en: The Mīmāṃsā Darśana; First Chapter, First Quarter.
Now, therefore, begins the inquiry into Dharma. || 1 ||
In the Śābarabhāṣya: "Those words which are well-known in common usage for certain meanings, those [are to be understood] in the Bṛhatī."
The *Śābarabhāṣya-ṭīkā* composed by Prabhākaramiśra:
Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma.
Regarding the commentary beginning with "In the world" (*loke*), it refers to the two words "Now, therefore" (*athātaḥ*) as being non-worldly (*alaukika*).

The purpose [of this inquiry] is the removal of doubt regarding the necessity [of the Vedas]. Why is this so? Because the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*) has been shown not to have an unintended meaning (*avivakṣitārtha*). But how, then, could there be a doubt that the meaning is unintended? Because no specific qualification (*adhikāra*) is heard in the injunction for the study of one's own Veda, and because it is prompted by the injunction for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇa-vidhi*). But how, then, [is it prompted] by another?

Is there an impulsion by something other than the injunction? If it is argued that this is like the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, we say no; for in those cases, it is appropriate because there is no difference in their own respective entitlements (*adhikāra*).

If it is argued that here too the element of entitlement does not differ, we say no, because there is no relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅga-aṅgin*) between them. But how, then, can there be subordination?

Is there not [the question of] being employed? Being employed is not the cause for being a subsidiary (*aṅga*). What then? It is application (*viniyoga*). But surely application is the cause for being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*); for it shows that only that which is applied is a subsidiary, as in the statement: "And that which is not prescribed does not become a subsidiary."

And as for the statement, "In the proximity of that which possesses a fruit, that which lacks a fruit is its subsidiary," it is not so; for being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*) alone is what is called subsidiariness.
That which functions to assist another, whether in its production or in its activity, is said to be for the sake of another.

And that alone is the constituent part (*aṅga*). Therefore, the status of being a constituent part is established solely by application (*viniyoga*), not by the act of employment (*prayukti*). But how can singularity and so forth be constituent parts? For it has been stated that the animal is a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) with respect to the act of procurement (*upādāna*); and that [status] was established by employment. Yet even that is certainly not established by employment. What then? It is established solely by application. But surely—

The meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) is determined by the case-endings (*vibhakti*), but singularity and so forth are not the meanings of the case-endings themselves. [Page 004] True, they are not determined [by the case-endings]; however, it is not the case that they are not understood even when [the stem] is employed as something already determined.

By means of case-endings (*vibhakti*). The oneness and other qualities of that which is enjoined are expressed by case-endings, because there is no comprehension of what is unconnected. For this very reason, there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) between the injunction of number and the injunction of the case-ending.
Therefore, it is correct that oneness and so forth are subordinate to the act of "taking up" (*upādāna*). However, the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana*) is not...

Nor is it understood as residing in that which is already enjoined; therefore, it is established that it is something to be employed (*prayojya*), not a subordinate element (*aṅga*). But how can that which is unenjoined and unrelated be implied? Enjoining is certainly not the cause of implication. What then? It is the task (*kārya*). Even that which resides in what is already enjoined is implied by the task alone.

The reason for being a subordinate member (*aṅga*) is its dependence on another (*tātsthya*). Furthermore, as it has been stated: "That which is not prescribed does not become a subordinate member," and "[regarding] the fruit...

And as for the statement, "In the presence of the calf, that limb [of the ritual] is fruitless," this passage is intended to establish that [the act] is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) with respect to the *kārya* (the task to be accomplished); it is not, however, intended to establish its status as a subordinate element (*aṅgatva*) [in the sense of being a constituent part of the sacrifice]. For desire (*kāma*) possesses the quality of being employed within the context of the qualification (*adhikāra*), yet it does not possess the status of a subordinate element (*aṅgatā*).

Therefore, being something to be employed (*prayojyatva*) is one thing, and being a subordinate element (*aṅgatā*) is another. Thus, while there is the state of being something to be employed for the words to be modified (*ūhyapada*), there is no status as a subordinate element (*śeṣatā*); for it is by way of application (*viniyoga*) that a mantra is said to be a subordinate element, and the words to be modified do not constitute a mantra. Therefore, because they are things to be employed and yet lack the status of subordinate elements, [the rule] applies to the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana*).
The doubt is as follows: is there a single purpose because of being employed [for a common end], or are there distinct purposes because of not being subsidiary parts?

In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī), considering that there is a single purpose due to being employed, held that [the specific details] were not intended to be expressed. To refute that, [the author states] "Now, therefore" (athātaḥ).
Thus the author of the Sūtras has accepted these two words;

and it is understood from the very reading that this [opposed] meaning is not refuted by these two words, because this meaning was not previously set forth. Therefore, some might entertain the suspicion that there is a non-worldly (alaukika) meaning [implied]. Hence, [the word] *antarṇīta*—

Considering that two words are capable of refuting the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), the author of the Commentary says: "Those words which are well-known in common usage for certain meanings, it should be understood that, whenever possible, they possess those very same meanings in the aphorisms (*sūtras*).
"Their meaning is not to be constructed through ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) and the like, nor is it to be defined by technical convention (*paribhāṣita*).
Furthermore, it is understood that this does not merely refute suspicions regarding its non-worldly (transcendental) meaning; rather, it is a technical convention (*paribhāṣā*).
Because of the absence of effort and reverence.

"In this world, this word *atha* is seen to signify the commencement of a topic immediately following what has preceded it; yet here, no such preceding matter is perceived"—thus he reveals the objection that [the usage] is non-worldly (*alaukika*). "It must be so..."

He states this to show that the doubt is not devoid of logical justification: for the purpose of establishing [the meaning], one must investigate the context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth; for when what has been heard is not in accordance with reality, the mere fact of its being "heard" (*śrutatva*) is not the sole determinant. And that [context] and so forth—
[Page 007] "All this exists"—thus it has been said: "But that is the study of the Veda. For when that exists, it follows...

"It is appropriate"—thus speaks now the proponent of the study of Vedic recitation whose intended meaning has not been stated. You, therefore, consider the study of the Veda to have already occurred through a thorough investigation of the meaning of the entire system; that is incorrect.

Since the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (svādhyāya-adhyayana-vidhi) is prompted by the injunction for becoming a teacher (ācāryakaraṇa-vidhi), it is understood that its own literal meaning is not intended to be expressed.
Now, this aphorism [JS 1.1.1] may have an entirely unseen (adṛṣṭa) purpose, namely: "Having studied the Veda, immediately thereafter [one should engage in] the inquiry into Dharma.
Thus...

In that case, there would result the injunction of two distinct meanings: "having studied the Veda" and "immediately thereafter. If it were said, "having studied the Veda," then the inquiry into Dharma would be possible immediately after any other action as well; whereas if immediate succession is enjoined, it would follow that the inquiry could occur even prior to the study of the Veda. And [this cannot be] for something whose purpose is unperceived (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

The prescription of two meanings for a single sentence is possible in two ways. It is said: this Sūtra is certainly not for the sake of some unseen purpose (adṛṣṭārtha); it is commenced solely for the investigation of the meaning of the Veda. Why? Because the Teacher employed the word "atha" with reference to such an inquiry into Dharma as is not possible without the prior study of the Veda.
How so? "A manifold investigation of Vedic statements will be undertaken here. But surely, they are not intended to convey meaning—[p.

It has been stated that the study of the Veda is for the sake of its meaning (*tattvārtha*). Or rather, even if that were intended, what is the purpose of enjoining immediate succession preceded by the study of the Veda? For [the sequence] is established by itself. Moreover, this being the case, we do not here intend to enjoin a prohibition of the inquiry into *dharma* prior to the study of the Veda; for this is not a single sentence.
Before the study of the Veda, he will prohibit the inquiry into Dharma; and after it, he will prescribe immediate succession.

For in that case, the sentence would be split; for the mode of expression of one who prohibits the inquiry into Dharma before the study of the Veda is different from that of one who teaches immediate succession after it—[namely,] "the Veda..."

"In one [interpretation], 'without having studied' is enjoined while the immediate sequence is restated; in the other, the reverse is the case; and because the meaning is the same, he will state that they form a single syntactical unit.
For this very reason, no suspicion regarding an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) should be raised against the Sūtra. For what purpose?

What then of the Sūtra? From the injunction to study one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayanavidhi*), it follows immediately that there must be a cessation from staying with the teacher’s family (*guru-kula*). However, because [the Sūtra] is not an ancillary part [of that injunction], it is logical that it is intended for its own purpose; it is not the case that its meaning is unintended. This is the purpose of the Sūtra. Thus he says: "When the Veda has been studied, two things present themselves: returning from the teacher’s family..."

"One must study and the Vedic sentences must be investigated; for that purpose, one should not return from the teacher's house—how else could one investigate the Vedic sentences? This instruction is for this very reason.
"If it is so, then..."

In that case, the study of the Veda must precede the inquiry into Dharma; for the author of the Smṛti considers the study of the Veda to have its own literal meaning unintended— stating, "Having studied the Veda, one should perform the ceremonial bath."

Speaking thus, he says: "And this statement of the Smṛti is not unjust, because the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (svādhyāya-adhyayana-vidhi) has as its object that which is already enjoined, and because [the Smṛti] is preceded by that."

Because [the word] conveys its own meaning. Therefore, it is logical that the Veda is understood as having its own meaning unintended for communication. "And the sacred tradition (āmnāya) must not be transgressed. To this it is said: "We shall indeed transgress this tradition;
by not transgressing it, we would be imagining the Veda—which actually possesses meaning—to be meaningless."

The injunction for becoming a teacher does not imply that the comprehension of meaning is necessarily required merely from the act of study. But surely, since it is impossible for the injunction to study one's own Veda (*svādhyāya-adhyayana-vidhi*) to have two purposes simultaneously, the meaning must simply not be intended (*avivakṣā*). To whom was this said?
Is this the purpose of the injunction for the study and recitation of one's own Veda? For its visible purpose is indeed the comprehension of ritual action.
And it has been stated that the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya-adhyayana*) is exhaustive [in its application], because no specific qualification for it is heard in the scriptures.

Regarding this, he says: "The venerable ritualists do not declare any fruit from mere study in that context; and even where they seem to declare one, there too—regarding substances, purificatory acts, and rituals—"
"Because it is for the sake of another, the mention of the fruit must be an explanatory statement (arthavāda)"— thus he will state its status as an arthavāda.
[Page 012] But surely no contradiction exists here; what then is the purpose of a sūtra intended to refute a contradiction?
How is there no contradiction? It is not the case that for one who has studied the Veda, this immediate sequence of bathing is being enjoined; nor...

For there is no word here that expresses immediate sequence (*ānantarya*); indeed, the suffix *-ktvā* is traditionally taught to denote priority in time, not immediate sequence. Moreover, if it were taken as immediate sequence, the visible purpose of study would be contradicted.
This might be so.

If there were another basis for this traditional teaching (*smṛti*), its source would simply be the completion of the injunction regarding the appointment of a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*), since that injunction concludes with the "recitation of the Veda" (*vedānuvacana*). However, "this meaning [of the *smṛti*] would have to be understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Why is it said that "this meaning would have to be understood through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā)"? This is explained as follows: "This bathing is not enjoined for the sake of an unseen spiritual merit (adṛṣṭa); rather, they say that by secondary indication, the conclusion of the observances such as abstaining from bathing coincides with the completion of Vedic study—'having studied the Veda, one should bathe.'"
—thus.

Therefore, in order to state that this [tradition] is rooted in logic (*nyāyamūlatā*), the Sūtra says: “Let him not return from the teacher’s house (*gurukula*). And if there were another root [for this tradition],...

An unseen principle (adṛṣṭa) would have to be postulated for memory; therefore, in order to avoid such an unseen purpose, the injunction regarding the appointment of a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*) alone is its root. Thus: "Therefore, having first completed the study of the Veda, dharma should subsequently be desired to be known."

It is established by the force of the employment of the word *atha*. If this is so, then this [employment] is not for an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*); nor is it for a seen purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), because that has already been attained; rather, only the departure from the teacher’s family (*gurukula*) is being prohibited. We do not say that there is no other action either—

The meaning of the word *atha* is not that "the desire to know dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*) should not be undertaken immediately after [studying the Veda]," but rather that "having studied the Veda, one should not bathe [to conclude one's student life] in haste; immediately thereafter, dharma is to be desired to be known."

Regarding the statement, “The word ‘therefore’ (ataḥ) indicates what has preceded by way of a reason,” what preceding factor does it indicate as being the cause? We reply: it is the study of the Veda. But how is the study of the Veda the cause?

Since it is observed that the comprehension of meaning follows immediately after the study [of the Veda], therefore, as with the study itself, the desire to know dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*) follows immediately after it.
This is what is expressed by the word "atha" (now/therefore). Thus, study is the cause for the desire to know dharma, insofar as it ensures its immediate succession.

The word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) in the previously mentioned sentence—"Just as this country is secure and well-supplied with food, therefore I dwell in this country"—indicates causality, thereby demonstrating its worldly meaning.
Likewise, it is understood that the Veda thus studied is the cause for the desire to know Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*); immediately thereafter, Dharma is to be investigated.
"One must sit"— thus he has demonstrated the very explanation of the word *atha* (thereupon) in order to make its status as a cause understood:
"For one who has not studied the Veda would not be able to investigate the Vedic sentences for the sake of Dharma."
By this,
he shows that his intention to speak is devoid of personal interest; "for this reason, immediately after this, [he will explain] the Dharma..."
"One should desire to investigate" is the meaning of the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*).
This is the concluding statement: "One should desire to investigate dharma...
To which portion of the Sūtra does the phrase "micchet" refer? We reply: it is the explanation of the term *dharmajijñāsā*.
But surely, one ought to say "dharmaṃ jijñāset"; for between the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*), the suffix—

The general rule is that the meaning of the suffix is predominant; however, in the compound *dharmajijñāsā*, this effort is made to demonstrate the predominance of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). [It is explained as: "the desire to know for the sake of Dharma is *dharmajijñāsā*.
But how so? [Because] the meaning of the base...

The meaning of the suffix is knowledge (*jñāna*), while the meaning of the desiderative suffix (*san*) is desire (*icchā*); it is precisely in such a sense that *san* is prescribed by the rule "after a verbal root denoting an action" (*dhātoḥ karmaṇaḥ*).
If this is so, then knowledge is primary, not the property (*dharma*). For [the property] does not have any other purpose.
Since action (*kriyā*) is the primary element, it is the inquiry into dharma alone that is primary. Therefore, the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) has dharma as its object.
This is what [the author] says: “For that is the desire to know it.
Thus, the inquiry into dharma has been stated.
Furthermore, how is that Dharma to be investigated? One must inquire: what is the Dharma; what are its characteristics; what are its means of realization;
what are the fallacious means of realization; and what is its ultimate purpose. For as long as the Dharma is not understood in this way, it cannot be practiced.
It is not sufficient; a dharma that is not practiced does not perform the function of dharma—so it has been said:
"The summary of these propositions is this aphorism: 'Now, therefore, the inquiry into dharma'."

What is this so-called "having the person as the ultimate goal"? This is stated with reference to the specific context: "Where is there the state of having the person as the ultimate goal, and where is the person subordinate?"
And thus it is said.
And what is the intended meaning of the statement: "Is this dharma well-known or unknown"?
If, however, this matter is understood from the Veda alone, what is there left to be investigated? True;

yet some great sages are in disagreement, describing the meaning as being preceded by other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), while others maintain that even the Mantras and Arthavādas possess authority according to their literal sense, even regarding matters that are not actions to be performed.

Those who assert that the Veda is the authoritative means of knowledge—since this disagreement exists, an inquiry (jijñāsā) is commenced for the sake of comprehending reality. An object not understood according to its true nature, when put into practice, ruins the practitioner; whereas, when practiced after being known, it unites one with the supreme good (niḥśreyasa). Thus, the inquiry is commenced, for [it precedes] all investigations.
Because it is preceded by a formal proposition, that is stated as follows: "Dharma is a matter characterized by an injunction (*codanā*). An "injunction" is that which impels one toward action.

"they say [it is] speech"—thus he shows that the Veda is authoritative regarding matters to be accomplished (*kāryārtha*). By stating "Dharma is characterized by that," he shows that it consists solely of the nature of what is to be accomplished. For "cognition is indeed of an existing thing."
Thus:
if the authority of the Veda pertains only to an object that is to be accomplished (kārya), how then is there the comprehension of objects that have already come into being (bhūta) and so forth?

[Is this so] regarding the mantras and arthavādas? For even their status as having purposeful action (kāryārthatā) will be explained in the second pāda. As it has been said: "It is capable of making [the meaning] understood. Nor is this meaning cognizable through other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
He shows that "there is no other faculty whatsoever. [Objection: "But would one not speak even of an object that is not as it is?
[Page 024]

By stating that the word "danā" lacks contact with its referent (*arthāsaṃsparśitā*), he points out a flaw in the thesis (*pratijñādoṣa*). But how does a word lack contact with its referent? It is said: for that which lacks contact with its referent is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); of that...

When a subverting cognition (*bādhakajñāna*) has arisen, a counter-cognition (*pratipakṣavijñāna*) does not arise again with that very same object as its cause. However, in the case of sound, even when a subverting cognition is clear, a counter-cognition arises again with sound itself as its cause—as in: "A herd of elephants exists on the tip of a finger. It is not so in the case of mother-of-pearl and silver.

The occurrence of this matter [of non-correspondence] is impossible. Therefore, because the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) does not touch upon the actual object, the thesis that "Dharma is characterized by it" is untenable.
To this it is replied: it is strange to say that it makes an object known and yet is non-tangential to the object.
If, first of all, this non-tangentiality is understood through a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-jñāna*), then it is certainly not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

It is produced; we shall demonstrate that it is a memory-cognition because its specific features are not apprehended. In the case of the Veda, however, since there is no subverting cognition (*bādhakajñāna*), even the suspicion that it does not correspond to reality does not exist. But surely, even when a subverting cognition exists, in the case of worldly sentences, knowledge arises from the word itself due to its status as the cause—[as in the case of] "an elephant at the tip of a finger."

Regarding the phrase "a hundred herds"—the suspicion that it does not touch upon the actual object has already been set aside. It is not so; you are ignorant of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator. In the statement "a hundred herds of elephants on the tip of a finger," there is here the observation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).
It is sublated, but not by a hundred herds of elephants. Thus he says:
"And it speaks, yet it is false. For this very reason, [the Sūtra states]: "If that [statement] comes from a trustworthy person..."
—Thus it has been said.
For the statement of one who is trustworthy is non-deviant and preceded by another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), provided that its object is perceptible.

But where the two are absent, there is error due to the subversion of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Regarding the meaning of a sentence, however, there is no such error. Why, then, is there error in human speech due to the subversion of other means of valid cognition? Because it is known— [p.

Men employ sentences in order to communicate a meaning to another; and since an unperceived object cannot become known, there must be a human statement that accords with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is what [the author] says:
"For it is impossible for that to be known by a person without [the aid of] a statement."

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might object: "Indeed, it is impossible for a person to know that without another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)"—this being what ought to be stated, what is the meaning of saying "except for the word" (ṛte vacanāt)?
[Question: What is meant by "mostly"? [Answer: It is said: indeed, even if it has a purposeful meaning, does it not follow that the word is still of human origin?

To refute this, it is stated: "without knowing [the object] apart from the word. [Objection: But in this way, the fact that [the Veda] is corroborated by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not demonstrated. [Reply: Certainly it is demonstrated; for it is shown that [the Veda] is free from dependence on other authorities.

The specific example is given, however, for the purpose of establishing that there is no dependence on anything invariably concomitant. Now, it may be objected: if it is said "without a statement," does it not follow that the *codanā* is indeed of human origin? It is replied: because of the statement—[p.

When this is said, the independence of the word with respect to its objective (kāryārtha) is indeed established. Therefore, it is proven that even within the lineage of persons (puruṣaparamparā), Dharma is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). But how is this proven? It can be inferred that there must be some means of apprehension (upalambhaka) because the instruction handed down through the lineage of persons would otherwise be inexplicable; however, [it cannot be inferred that such a means is perceptible].

[Objection: There is independence of the word [of scripture]. [Reply: This is not so; for instruction arises even from delusion, and when there is no delusion, it arises even from the Veda. Since these two bases are possible, one cannot say that there exists another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) apart from those enumerated. Therefore, because the occurrence of a contrary [cognition] through another means of valid cognition is impossible, [the scripture is authoritative].
Furthermore, it can be asserted that the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) does not, by its own nature, touch upon the actual object. Therefore, the proposition has been well stated:
“Dharma is an object characterized by the Vedic injunction.
Moreover, [this is so] because of human speech.

The certainty arises that "this meaning has been understood by this person," but no further cognition of another means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is produced. As it has been said: "Moreover, from a human statement, the conviction arises that 'this person knows it thus,' but not that 'the object is thus.'"

How is it that the apprehension of another means of valid cognition occurs upon the apprehension of a different object? Certainly; for in that case, the means of valid cognition is conceived as following after the object.

[Objection: But is it not the case that even this "he knows" (*veda*) must be postulated? [Reply: No, because consciousness has a well-known cause, whereas the object has no established basis. Even the cognition "he knows" does not arise from the word of a person, since mental distractions (*vikṣepa*) are possible; how much less so regarding the object itself? He shows this: "Indeed, some person even errs..."

"From the statement that [the cognition] arises from what has been done"—is this "inference based on general observation" (sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa)? Since both types [of inference] have already been refuted, what else remains by which it could be said: "Is it not indeed an inference based on general observation"?
Is this so? It is true that it is so; however, in another context, he considers the inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) to be unrefuted:
"Indeed, even some person may err regarding a statement composed by another person."

Thus it has been said: "In that case, the meaning is one way, while the cognition from the word is another way"; this [objection] becomes consistent with the facts. What is the logical ground for this? Indeed, the consequence follows that a word does not touch its object because it is a word, just like a word whose meaning is distorted. True.

If words are erroneous because they lack correspondence with reality (*ayathārthatva*), [this is so] only when the object of that which lacks correspondence with reality is understood from the word; it does not follow from the mere fact of lacking correspondence with reality. This has been stated: "No, because of its difference"—meaning, it is different.

This very [fact of being produced by words] would be the reason for the word's lack of correspondence with its object regarding the referent. Furthermore, even if the distortion arises from the word itself, this inference still does not hold; for the statement of a reason must depend upon the apprehension of a thesis (pratijñā) whose subject (pakṣa) is unimpaired.
Furthermore, this position is faulty because cognition (*saṃvit*) is perceptible (*pratyakṣa*). This has been stated: “But the cognition [of dharma] is perceptible through the words of the Veda.
Cognition (*pratīti*) is what is meant by *pratyaya*. Now, dharma is certainly not something to be produced (*kārya*); what then is it?

[This is] a quality (*guṇa*). Thus, some consider it a quality of the intellect (*dhī*), while others consider it a quality of the self (*ātman*). Therefore, the statement that "an injunction (*codanā*) is a word that prompts action, and dharma is the object characterized by that" is the [correct] formulation.

This is not tenable, because *dharma* is not something that is produced as an effect. Therefore, in order to refute that [objection], the author of the *Bhāṣya* introduced [the definition] by way of a summary in that context, stating: "Therefore, *dharma* is that which brings about the highest good," and so forth.

But how is the refutation accomplished? Because the relationship between word and meaning is understood through worldly usage (*lokavyavahāra*), [it is established] regarding the sense of what is to be done (*kāryārtha*).
Ordinary people employ the word *dharma* in such ways as, "He who performs a sacrifice," and so forth.

This has been demonstrated. For the purpose of showing the connection and the utility of the word *artha*, the author of the Bhāṣya stated: “Both the beneficial (*artha*) and the harmful (*anartha*) are indicated here by the injunction (*codanā*);
and furthermore, this was stated again following a question:

“What is the beneficial? That which leads to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and others. What is the harmful? That which leads to transgression (*pratyavāya*), such as the Śyena sacrifice and others.
Thus, the nature of dharma and adharma has been stated as being characterized by the attainment of the supreme good and the occurrence of transgression. And so—
By demonstrating both, it is stated that they are characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanā-lakṣaṇa*).
In that case, how could only that which leads to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) possess the nature of Dharma, while that which is a cause of transgression (*pratyavāya*) does not?
“Let it not be so”—this [objection] is indeed improper. [The opponent asks: “But how can that which is harmful (anartha) be taught as something to be done?
[The author replies: How can that which is not taught as something to be done yet be characterized by the Vedic injunction (codanālakṣaṇa)? How?

Is the connection with the word *artha* (purposeful object) intended to exclude from the status of *dharma* that which, though characterized by an injunction (*codanālakṣaṇa*), is not purposeful? Furthermore, he clarifies this again in the subsequent passage: “The Śyena and other such [sacrifices] are certainly not understood as things to be performed.”

[Page 037] Since they are not taught as things to be performed (*kartavyatā*) and yet are characterized by injunction (*codanālakṣaṇa*), a certain difficulty appears to arise. Furthermore, as for the question: "But how is this [non-existence] a harm (*anartha*)?"
Having raised the question thus, it was stated: "For that [action] is indeed violence, and that is prohibited.
This too is contradictory from beginning to end; for [it is said]: "He who [commits] transgression..."

Having stated that "undesirability" consists in the characteristic of transgression (*pratyavāya*), he has further stated that it consists in the characteristic of prohibition (*pratiṣedha*). Therefore, there is an inconsistency. Now, if it is argued that there is no contradiction even between prohibition and transgression, [regarding] the transgression—
Because it functions as a cause for negation, that is incorrect; for the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) has no other purpose.
Indeed, the rule of negation culminates solely in the meaning of the negative particle itself; it is not capable of making known that the meaning of that [negation] has some other purpose.
To this, it is said: This objection arises from one who has not determined the operation of *niyoga*.

*Niyoga* has "that which is to be done" (*kartavyatā*) as its object; it does not, however, express "that which is to be done" itself. If so, how was it stated that the Veda possesses authority regarding an object that is a task (*kārya*)?
This is correct, because the *niyoga* (the mandate) has that as its object. What is this relationship between object and subject?
That in which this person is enjoined is the object of that [mandate]. Therefore, the injunction does not express that [the act] is to be performed; rather, it does so by way of being its object.

It appropriates. Therefore, whatever is appropriated is that which is to be enjoined; such is the conventional usage in the *tantra*. That which functions as the cause of appropriation is the basis for the qualification (*adhikāra*). Thus, having accepted its status as the occasion for qualification, this— [p.
It has been said: "For that [act] is indeed violence, and it is prohibited.

For a prohibition concerning the materials [of the sacrifice] would be for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*), not one concerning the qualification [of the agent]. "One should not harm living beings."

Thus, this prohibition pertains to the qualification for the rite and serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*); therefore, it is capable of establishing that malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) is harmful, but not so the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice and others, because those serve the purpose of the ritual (*kratvartha*). Now, why is this prohibition not for both purposes?—"Not [to kill]..."
"Should one harm living beings"? For it is not possible for a single injunction to possess both the quality of being an instigator and the quality of not being an instigator.

Now, why does this [injunction] not serve the purpose of the ritual (*kratvartha*)? Between the two states of being an instigator and not being an instigator, [the former] is the state of being an instigator.

It is based on direct Vedic revelation (*śrauta*), because its understanding is independent [of other means]; however, its non-prescriptive nature is understood through the consideration of another sentence.
And there is no such understanding from another sentence as "one should not harm living beings."

Because it is prescribed without reference [to a specific ritual context], this prohibition pertains specifically to the *adhikāra* (the qualified person’s entitlement). And it is indeed characterized by an injunction (*codanālakṣaṇa*), because the injunction regarding the Śyena sacrifice has that very thing as its object. Therefore, "both are here indicated by the injunction."
Thus, the commentary beginning with these words has a logically established meaning.
[p. 041] "But surely this sūtra is incapable [of its purpose]."

— This is for the purpose of demonstrating the distinction between worldly and Vedic sentences. [The phrase] “Now, of an existing object”— this indicates that even according to the sentence, there is a single meaning.
In order to demonstrate that it arises.
“The investigation of its cause” refers to the occasion for stating the reason.
But how is it that, regarding an object that is a product (*kāryārtha*), the injunction alone is the means of knowledge? Because other means, such as perception and the like, are impossible.
How are they impossible?

“When there is contact with an existing object, the arising of cognition for a person through the sense organs is perception; it is not a means [for knowing dharma], because it is the apprehension of what is already present.
Now, why is inference and the rest not a means? Regarding inference and the others—

For validity regarding its own object is preceded by the apprehension of a causal sign (*nimitta*), and in this case, that sign is precisely the phonemes and so forth, which are perceivable by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); therefore, even that [verbal cognition] is not a valid means of knowledge. But is it not the case that verbal testimony as a means of knowledge is indeed dependent upon other means of knowledge?

Worldly transaction is observed. True; it is observed as the object of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but it is not dependent upon another means of valid cognition; for the innate power of a word resides in its own referent. As it has been said:
Regarding the phrase "But it is innate" (*autpattikastu*),
the introduction of this alternative interpretation— "The author of the *Vṛtti*, however,
explained this passage in another way"— for what purpose? If it were for the sake of refutation...

Generally speaking, that is incorrect, because it expresses the meaning correctly. If it is argued that the acceptance of those [three] sūtras is for the purpose of demonstrating a different meaning, then even in that case, the mention of the author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*) is inappropriate. Or rather, what would not be established even without stating a different meaning? It is said: both faults exist—the fault of a different meaning...

And as for the statement: "What is refuted here? First of all, the claim that 'an examination of the cause should not be performed' is improper, because the negative particle (*nañ*) is not heard [in the original], and because the sense of existence is eternally present. As for the statement of the reason—
As for the claim that "the means of valid cognition are well-known," that too is incorrect, because we observe disagreements regarding them. By oneself—

It has been said: "But surely perception is fallible. However, its non-fallibility was stated by means of an examination of its causes. And that very point was proposed by the author of the Sūtras as the subject to be examined; how then [could it be otherwise]?

Is the supply of the negative particle (*nañ*) appropriate? It must be stated that it serves to refute the absence of an objective basis (*nirālambanatā*), yet this was not mentioned by the author of the *Vṛtti*; therefore, it is a flaw. Furthermore, what other distinct meaning (*arthāntara*) remains to be stated?
[The answer is: another distinct meaning has been stated by him in order to demonstrate a further proof for the meaning of the three preceding Sūtras.
And likewise, there is a transposition of the words "tat" and "satoḥ," as well as the statement of the definition for all means of valid cognition.

Furthermore, at the end of the definition of perception, it is stated: "That cognition alone is incorrect for which the instrument is defective and for which there is a subsequent conviction that it is false; no other."
—This is the restriction.

What is being restricted by this? It is said: that for which these two do not exist is restricted as not being a false cognition (*mithyā-pratyaya*). But what is that? It is that which arises through association with name, genus, and so forth.
And this [external object] does not exist for it. Furthermore, others do not accept that this [cognition] has a different object as its support;
rather, they maintain that its object is precisely what was cognized by non-conceptual [perception], asserting that "this is merely conceptual construction. He...

And thus it is said that this is conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). Even in this established doctrine, conceptual cognitions (*savikalpaka*)—such as the cognitions of universals (*jāti*) and so forth—are not held to have as their objects only those things already cognized by non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-pratyaya*). However, there is this much difference:

The distinction is as follows: even in this case, the status of being an object cognized by indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyaya*) does not depart from the object due to its connection with a previously experienced thing. Furthermore, it cannot be said that the determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*) has a different object simply because the cognition of connection itself connects with another object; therefore, [the determinate cognition] does not have a different object.

A false apprehension does not arise for him, because of the non-existence of duality. Therefore, this restriction made for that purpose appears to yield a rather meager result. But was it not said by you yourself: "However, there is this distinction"?

For this specific reason, others have stated as follows: because it does not have as its object another thing that is connected with the object being synthesized, the object is not apprehended as the domain of this cognition in its capacity as a unique, self-referential entity;
rather, it attains the status of an objective support (*ālambana*). Therefore, the synthesizing cognition does not possess the nature of a determiner (*paricchedaka*).

They say it is like memory. And in this established conclusion (rāddhānta), the validity even of conceptual cognition (savikalpaka) is accepted. Nor is it established that even for opponents who maintain that there is only conceptualization (vikalpamātra) regarding the synthetic cognition (anusandhāna-pratyaya), these two [conditions] exist. Therefore, for one who desires the validity of this [synthetic cognition], this restriction is superfluous. How so?

Furthermore, do they consider conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) to be the cognition of synthesis? Because there is no difference between the genus (*jāti*) and that which possesses the genus (*jātimat*), and because a distinction is admitted in the cognition of synthesis; for common people understand it as "this is a cow," and not as "this [is a genus]."

"A substance possessing cowness"—thus [it is said]. Now, it may be argued that even when there is a cognition of difference, a metaphorical identification (abhedopacāra) is observed, as in the expression, "Bring in the spears. True, there is a metaphorical identification; however, in the case of "This is a cow," ordinary people do not have a conceptual understanding of it as being figurative. Therefore, it cannot be asserted that this cognition is merely metaphorical.
Furthermore, this cognition does not terminate in the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), because it involves a subsequent synthesis of other things.
Therefore, we consider that this is merely a conceptual construction (*parikalpanā*). If this cognition were to apprehend things otherwise [than they are], [it would be erroneous].
How is it that there is no error? For there is no error in the cognition regarding cows and the like. It is said:

Error occurs only where one substance is apprehended as having the nature of another substance; however, this [universal] such as "cowness" is not a different substance, because it is not perceived as distinct from the individuals, unlike blue, yellow, and so forth. Since...

For it is precisely in this way that particulars are apprehended by means of a universal; and for this very reason, those who know conceptual construction maintain that this cognition called "conceptual construction" (vikalpa) is distinct from both valid cognition (pramāṇa) and error (viparyaya). [p. 056] Guṇakalpa...

Nor has this [superimposition] been explained by that [previous analysis], because name is not mentioned separately. But is it not the case that name is indeed mentioned separately? No; for even there, in the cognition "This is Viṣṇumitra," there is a perception of non-difference. However, this is the distinction between the conceptualizations of genus and quality: in one case (genus), there is a conceptualization of difference between two things that are non-different; in the other case (quality), there is a conceptualization of non-difference between two things that are different.

No; therefore, this is a distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), not a distinction of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). But surely, in the case of a conceptual construction of action, neither of these two is possible, for a relationship is understood only between two distinct things—action and its agent—and they are also designated as such. Not so; even here, it is precisely a metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) that is understood.

And it is designated [as such], as in "Devadatta cooks," because we observe grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). But is it not also observed that there is lack of coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), as in "He cooks rice," "He cooks with wood," and "It is cooked by Devadatta"?

Thus it is asked: "What is this being prattled—'because a difference of substratum is observed'? For a difference of substratum is observed even in the case of universals (*jāti*) and so forth: "the state of being a cow is cowness," "the whiteness of a cloth," or "this is its name.

This designation [of a difference of substratum] applies to that which is non-different [from the universal], provided one entertains the conceptualization of it as both different and non-different; it does not, however, apply to that which is actually different.
Furthermore, there is no introduction of a separate entity; therefore, this too is merely a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), as in the expression "Devadatta cooks.
The same applies to substances, as in "this man is staff-bearing," due to the metaphorical attribution of non-difference (*abhedopacāra*). Therefore, this [metaphorical designation] is fivefold.

Conceptual construction (*kalpanā*): this is neither a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) nor a non-means of valid cognition. It is said: conceptual knowledge does exist, provided that knowledge were to be apprehended through perception (*pratyakṣa*); however, he will state that knowledge is inferential (*ānumānika*). [Objection: But if the position is that knowledge is not perceptible, then it is untenable for knowledge to arise in one way while its objective support (*ālambana*) has a different form.
What is this "being otherwise" (*anyathābhāva*)? This is what "being otherwise" means: for mother-of-pearl appears as if it were silver.
That cognition indeed has mother-of-pearl as its object (*ālambana*), not silver. How is this understood?
Because [the error] occurs when the eye is in contact with mother-of-pearl, and because it does not arise in one who is blind;
for a blind person does not designate mother-of-pearl as "silver," whereas only one who possesses sight thinks of mother-of-pearl as "silver," [thinking], "My eye is in close proximity to silver."
Thus, this cognition has the mother-of-pearl as its objective support, not silver. And this is not possible in the case of a cognition that is not perceptual.

Therefore, it should be understood that there exists cognition even when its objective support (*ālambana*) is a non-existent form. This is the fivefold conceptualization (*kalpanā*). Now, one might object: "If the position is that cognition has a non-existent form as its objective support, then it follows that cognition is entirely without an objective support (*nirālambana*). It is not so; for in the case of being without an objective support, there would be no designation of it by means of anything else.

It is possible; and there is indeed the designation "silver" with respect to mother-of-pearl. For, on the view that cognition is without an objective basis (*nirālambana*), how could there be a designation of one thing by another, given that the cognitions of mother-of-pearl and silver are distinct?
But surely, even on the view that cognition has an objective basis (*sālambana*), an object of a different form can be the basis for a cognition of a different form.

This is not tenable. For this alone constitutes the status of an object as an object (*ālambana*), namely that it produces a cognition having its own form; otherwise, even though it were active, like the eye and other sense organs, it would not be an object.

In the arising of knowledge, there would be no designation of an objective support (*ālambana*). Who has said that this conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is independent of both the objective support and the mental aspect (*ākāra*)? How, then, is it a conceptual construction? By way of connecting with another object (*arthāntarānusandhānatayā*). What does "by way of connecting with another object" mean? It means this and that—*idam idam*.

That which is the attainment of oneness with another particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of difference upon itself. How then are cognitions of universals (*jāti*) and so forth said to have non-existent objects? For they are called "having non-existent objects" because of the superimposition of difference and non-difference, which do not exist in the particular characteristic itself. What is this so-called superimposition (*adhyāsa*)? It is the [non-apprehension of] distinction...

[Page 062] There is the apprehension [of the object]; because there is only the apprehension of its own form (svarūpa) and no consideration of its differences, there is the superimposition of a universal (sāmānyādhyāsa).

Furthermore, there is a similarity between that which is non-different and another object; because there is no consideration of this similarity, there is the superimposition of difference (bhedādhyāsa).
Non-apprehension of similarity, however, arises from the non-connection with distinctions. This is the fivefold conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
Nor does it have a form distinct from its objective support (*ālambana*). Rather, it is colored by the connection with another object;
yet, one object cannot be the objective support for another object through such a connection. Therefore, [it is called conceptual construction] because of the connection with another object.

Even that which has a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object is called conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Therefore, it is only within the position of self-cognizing knowledge (*svasaṃvedya-jñāna*) that the experience of the distinctness of cognitions is logically established, even when they have the same object; otherwise, there would be only the object itself.

There would be only the cognition of a word, not the cognition of a particular (svalakṣaṇa) or a universal (sāmānya). Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that there is no universal distinct from the particular—because another form is not apprehended, and because when that [particular] is not apprehended, there is an absence of its cognition—and also because of the synthesis (anusandhāna) of a different object. And such synthesis is possible only when there is a difference in cognitions.

The worldly conventional usage of generalities and particulars is thus established; and in this way, the erroneous apprehensions that are the causes of saṃsāra— namely, the notion of permanence in the impermanent, the notion of pleasure in the unpleasant, and the notion of self in the non-self— are established.
This is what was stated: “How is this understood prior to the arising of a subverting cognition?”—
this refers to the cognition of the general and the particular with the intention that they have a single objective basis.

For it is impossible for a cognition with a different object to arise when the eye is associated with something else, because it does not arise in one who is blind—as has been stated. For this very reason, it is said: "The object is not of a different form...

"It is the cause for the arising of a cognition that has another form"—this is what [the opponent] means. How then do misconceptions such as "self" and so forth arise with respect to what is not-self? It is said in reply: a cognition that has arisen, having apprehended another similar object while failing to grasp the distinction [between it and the actual object], becomes the cause for a recollective cognition regarding that other similar object.

"I remember"—this refers to one who is devoid of such knowledge. Indeed, cognitions of silver and the like with respect to mother-of-pearl and so forth have already been established. But how is it in the case of dreams and the like, which concern what is not the self?

Having first stated the distinction of dreams and the like from those previously mentioned, we shall now state their lack of distinction regarding theories that deny an external object (*nirālambanavāda*).

He will state later: "And in the doctrine of the Self, regarding non-self and so forth. Therefore, the cognition of genus and the like is not caused by superimposition (adhyāsa) based on the mental connection with a distinct object. As for the argument that—because another form is not perceived, there is an absence of its cognition when that [other form] is not grasped—

This has been stated, but that is unproven; for the cognition that reflects upon another object is intended to be distinct from the cognition of the specific particular (*svalakṣaṇa*). And for one who maintains that there is no cognition other than perception, that [distinctness] would result in being the object itself. Therefore, this is unproven:

"because another form is not apprehended, and because when that [object] is not apprehended, there is an absence of the cognition thereof. Thus, it is well said: "when [the sense organ] is in contact with something else..."

"Knowledge whose object is other than the visual organ is not perception. How, then, can there be error? We say: it is precisely because of non-apprehension (*agrahaṇa*). And the fact that non-apprehension is the cause has been shown by the author of the Bhāṣya: "If... [p. 067]
"The mind is impaired by the eyes and other [senses].
How is it shown by this that [the mind] is the cause of non-apprehension?
"[When consciousness has another object...]"

—thus [it is said], because this is presented as the reason for that proposition. And it is logical that being defective consists in the incapacity to produce an effect, rather than the capacity to produce another effect. Therefore, errors are indeed based solely on non-apprehension. Hence, it is established that: “And for whom...”* *Note: The sentence is incomplete in the source text.*
The instrument is defective, and that cognition wherein there is the conviction "this is false" is itself the incorrect cognition,
and no other.

[068] But surely every cognition is without an objective basis (*nirālambana*), like a dream; how then can there be its being associated with that [object] or its not being so associated, by which distinction a difference between perception and non-perception is apprehended?

But how, then, is every cognition devoid of an objective basis (*nirālambana*)? For the nature of cognition as being devoid of an objective basis is observed in dreams. [Objection: But surely the cognition of silver with respect to mother-of-pearl was declared to be a memory-cognition due to the loss [of the object], as in "I remember. [Reply: This is appropriate in the case of silver and the like; for in that instance, there is a luminous form in the mother-of-pearl.

It might be plausible that what is delimited by the eye serves as the awakener of the memory of silver; however, in dreams and the like, since nothing is being perceived at all, the avoidance of awakening a memory of some other object seems difficult to achieve. Therefore—

We maintain that this web of cognition is based solely upon latent impressions (*vāsanā*). From the perception of a similar object, there arises the awakening of memory regarding another similar object; as for dreams, it has been stated that they occur because nothing [external] is apprehended. Therefore, the postulation that latent impressions alone are the cause is the simpler one; there is no need to resort to another entity [as a cause], because such a view would be under-inclusive (*avyāpti*). Thus, [the dream-cognition does not arise from] a wall...
Even in dreams and similar states, cognition is caused solely by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and not by external objects such as walls; this is the established position. It is said in reply:
for a cause is postulated for the sake of accomplishing an effect, not for the sake of destroying the effect. And in dreams and so forth...
Consciousness manifests externally, and it occurs even in the absence of an external object.
That which cannot exist without something else must have that thing as its cause. Therefore, it is logical to conclude that the object itself is the cause.

Furthermore, the state of being without an objective support (nirālambanatā) is not perceived at all through direct sensory cognition. Consequently, knowledge born of the senses [is based on an external object].
It has been stated that it is not caused by latent impressions (*vāsanā*). But surely, for one who has awakened, the cognition arises: "What was perceived in the dream was false.

And it is not logical to postulate a cause for that which is false. Yet, is it not the case that even a false cognition cannot arise without a cause? True; however, that [postulation] does not accord with the actual understanding.

For if they were in accordance with that [reality], there would be no false cognition at all. Therefore, false cognitions are the cause of delusion, and the worldly latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are the basis of delusion. Thus, [the cycle] is bound by latent impressions.
This entire web of cognition has arisen as such from the perspective of those who know reality. But surely this has already been refuted:
"I remember"—these cognitions of memory are devoid of the object of cognition. But surely this is not so, because there is no possible cause for the awakening of memory.
It was stated that [the cause] is possible. That is unproven, for even in dreams and the like, there is the possibility of reflection (*cintā*), unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), and so forth;

indeed, pleasure and pain are experienced even in a dream, and the cause of pleasure and pain is the unseen merit/demerit. Therefore, it is established that while some dream-cognitions and the like have the unseen merit/demerit as their cause, others have reflection and the like as their cause; thus, their similarity to the cognition of mother-of-pearl and the like is logical.
Regarding the cognition of dreams and so forth, this has been stated: “How could the well-ascertained cognition of a waking person—‘this is a pillar’—be erroneous?
How is this expressed by that [statement]? It means that which is ascertained is delimited [as real].

How can an object that is delimited be undelimited? How, then, does one who has awakened know it to be "false"? It has been said: because of the loss of memory—thinking "I remember"—that [cognition] is equal to direct perception.

The conceit of direct perception does not depart for one who has awakened. He clarifies this very point: "Now, if the cognition [of an object] is the cause of its existence as such, it cannot be said that it is something other than the cognition itself.
And because it is a cognition,
one does not consider the understanding to be false; for the cognition of a dream [arises] from something else.
The phrase "whose state is false" shows that it is the cause of forgetfulness. Why? Because of the observation of the weakness of the sense faculties—as in, "My mind is overcome by sleep."
By such statements as these, it is stated that weakness (*daurbalya*) consists in the incapacity for an effect, not the capacity for the production of another effect.

But is it not the case that by stating "it is indeed empty," you have already proposed that very lack of objective support (*nirālambanatā*) by asserting the emptiness of the object of cognition; and has that [lack of support] not been refuted by your statement that [the cognition] is equivalent to the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell?
This very same refutation is raised once again. By what reasoning? Because consciousness has an object of cognition (*saṃvedya*).
And that [consciousness] belongs either to the self, or to the intellect (*buddhi*), or indeed to knowledge itself; it is logical that its object is that wherein it resides.
[Objection: Consciousness itself would thus become the object of cognition. Therefore, it is not capable of cognizing another object.

It must be understood that sound, touch, form, taste, and smell constitute the nature of consciousness, the self, or the intellect. Why do we not perceive any difference in form between the object and its cognition?

Is the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) intended here merely for the sake of illustration? No; for when the object of cognition rests within consciousness, only knowledge remains, because the intellect and the self are equivalent to sound and the other objects [in that they are both cognized]. Furthermore, consciousness is inseparable from knowledge. In the state of deep sleep, it [consciousness] [resides] in the self.

And because it is not observed in the case of cognition; for sleep is indeed the withdrawal of knowledge. Having considered this, it was said: "We do not perceive any difference in form between the object and its cognition."

—Thus [it is said]. But where has this been seen—that "the object alone is cognized by consciousness"? For we understand that something is an object of cognition precisely by virtue of its being cognized, not by virtue of its being an object.
Who indeed has said that "the state of being an object of cognition is understood through the state of being an object of cognition"? Rather, it is through consciousness...
Since that [consciousness] is directly perceived and its nature is that of knowledge, we consider that sound and the rest possess the very form of that [consciousness].

For who indeed would postulate the perceptibility of both consciousness and sound and so forth? Therefore, the established conclusion is that this collection of sound and the rest is nothing but the form of consciousness; there is no external object whatsoever.

[077] But would it not follow that consciousness (*saṃvit*) is non-conformable with its object? For if consciousness possesses the form of sound and so forth, the experience of the apprehended and the apprehender (*grāhyagrāhakasaṃvedana*) is not possible. Therefore, one must conclude that it is a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). And yet—

It is logical that conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is an object cognizable by all people. Furthermore, nothing in the world is observed to be expressible by the word "conceptual construction" unless it is permeated by a connection with another object. Therefore, it is better to accept the perceptibility of both [the object and the cognition], rather than denying the cognition itself; for if that were done, consciousness (*saṃvit*) would be lost, and whose [would be] this form consisting of words and so forth? This is logical.

If the cognition of the apprehended object and the apprehending subject were to exist by means of a different form (ākāra), we would perceive that other form; however, we do not perceive any other form, for it is only the form of blue and so forth that appears as both. And what is this appearance of both as a single form, if not the very act of appearing? Thus it has been said: "We do not perceive any difference in form between the object and the cognition."
Thus,
by the statement "and our cognition is perceptual," this is what is meant: and our consciousness is perceptual.

Thus, this form of blue and so forth is directly perceived. Therefore, this consciousness, possessing that form, appears in two ways. Consequently, it is established that this consciousness is devoid of an external object. Hence—due to its connection with that...
"This conviction regarding that [object]"—this is mere idle chatter. But what is the cause for this twofold appearance?
To this it has been replied: "We do not perceive any difference in form. As for the cause of the appearance, it is the appearance itself—
It must be understood that "the gods exist. And this latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) is beginningless—so it has been stated by the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*).
It is replied: the appearance of both [subject and object] is unestablished in the case of blue, yellow, and so forth; for that [appearance] occurs solely as the apprehended (*grāhya*).

It shines, but not as a subject (*grāhaka*). Rather, one perceives it simply as "the subject," not as "blue" or "yellow. This is what was said: "For that [cognition], connected with external space, is perceived through direct perception" (p.

Thus: "Perceptual cognition has an object as its domain, not cognition itself as its domain"—this shows that the appearance of form occurs solely by way of being the apprehended (*grāhya*), whereas the appearance of the apprehender (*grāhaka*) does not have form as its domain. What, then, is its domain? It is cognition itself. But [one might object]: surely no other form at all is perceived?

It has been stated: how, then, is there the introduction of another subject here? Indeed, this is a fault for one who maintains the doctrine of perception (*pratyakṣavādin*); however, for one who maintains the doctrine of inferential knowledge (*ānumānikajñānavādin*), this objection does not apply. Nor is it...

From the apprehension of form [arises] the inference that grasps only existence (*sanmātra*). But has it not been stated that consciousness (*saṃvit*) is perception? Consciousness is one thing, and the object of consciousness is another; if both were perceptible, there would have to be the perception of two forms, yet such is not the case. Therefore, this is precisely the denial of the object of consciousness.
[The opponent] maintains that this is logical. [The author replies: This is a lack of discernment on the part of the venerable one; for no difference in form (rūpāntara) is admitted in the fruit.

Indeed, if there were a cognition of a different form, it would result in two fruits; for a single cognition has only a single cognizable object as its domain, and it does not have two cognizable objects as its domain. Is cognition then non-cognizable? We do not say that cognition is not cognizable.

Thus it is said: consciousness is indeed to be known by consciousness itself, not by way of being an object of knowledge (*saṃvedyatayā*). What kind of verbal expression is this—to say that it is "to be known" and yet "not to be known"? This is the meaning of the expression: it possesses no state of being an object (*karmabhāva*). And an object is what is denoted by the term "to be known," not consciousness. Therefore, there is no separate object of knowledge.

It can be grasped by that [consciousness]. Nor is consciousness itself unperceivable, because the perceivability of all entities is rooted in it. What, then, is inferential here? For the result itself is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, the means of valid cognition—

People think thus. How do they think? They do not maintain that it is the fruit itself. What is the intention? For such is worldly convention (*laukiko vyavahāraḥ*). What is this "worldly convention"?
The meaning is that worldly people perceive these two forms. Therefore, the object is established.

There is a duality, because consciousness is not itself cognized, whereas the object is cognized. Is consciousness entirely uncognizable? Certainly it is uncognizable, but it is not unmeasurable. What, then, is the distinction between the measurable (*prameya*) and the cognizable (*saṃvedya*)? For where...

The essential nature of an object is delimited; that is called "cognizable. Therefore, those who know the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) maintain that self-cognition is perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, there is no cognition [of itself] within the knowledge that constitutes the result of a valid cognition, because no other form is apprehended. Consequently, it is incorrect to say that knowledge is perception. Moreover, because of its momentariness, its status as perception is not possible, [as is the case with] the fruit of the means of valid cognition.
Because it is not continuous. This is what he says: “For that [cognition] is momentary; it will not persist until the time of another cognition.
Now, the intention here is this: since cognition is itself of the nature of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it does not depend upon another means of valid knowledge.
Thus it has been said: "If it should be argued that 'this [cognition] is known precisely while it is arising, and it makes another object known, like a lamp'—[we reply:
it is true that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not depend on another means of valid cognition for its own apprehension (*pramiti*). And we..."

We recognize [the object] precisely as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because consciousness has that as its cause. Nor do we say that knowledge in that state is itself an object of another cognition; rather, the object of inference is simply that "that state exists," for it is impossible to know the existence of that which possesses the state if the state itself does not exist. This is what was stated: "Not..."
For when an object is unknown, no one perceives cognition; but once it is known, one understands it through inference.
In that case, simultaneity is untenable.
Thus [it is said]. But surely—the experts in the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) recollect the object of cognition (*prameya*) as "known.
True, they recollect it as "known," but not as "the known. As it has been stated:
"It is true that the cognition arises first, but it is not first cognized."

—Thus [it is said]. But surely this contradicts common worldly experience: people designate memory as "the jar was known yesterday," and not as "yesterday was the jar. True, it would be contradictory if this designation were always the case.
"For it sometimes happens that an object which is actually known is said to be 'unknown'. For in such a case [p.

The statement "it is known"—this refers to memory, which arises from the operation of two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, this statement—"and after the time of memory"—is devoid of discrimination.
Furthermore, if both were perceptible, then [the relation] of the cognition with the object...

Designation [of the cognition] is not possible, as it would be in the case of color and touch. Furthermore, there is no apprehension of the form of a cognition without the designation of an object. Therefore, perception does not have cognition as its object; rather, it has the object as its object. Consequently, it is established that cognition is inferential by virtue of its result. And this non-discrimination between the result and the object of knowledge is the means of valid cognition (*pramā*).

Because there is no interval, that [object] is logically its object. Therefore, it is more reasonable to deny the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) itself, rather than denying the object of cognition (*prameya*). Thus: "Granted, if there were only a single form, it would be the non-existence of the cognition itself, and not of the object."

"Of that which is directly perceived, there is no single uniformity; for we infer cognition to be indeed formless, yet we apprehend the object as possessing form through direct perception. Therefore, cognition has the object as its support.
What [is the reason]?

Furthermore, if one denies the result while admitting the cause, does this imply a denial of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) itself and not of the object of knowledge (*prameya*), since both are dependent upon the result? Not so; for it is in their *origination* that both are dependent upon the result, but not in their *cognition*.
In whose origination? For when the result is a means of making known, it is the object of knowledge alone that is to be known, not [the means] that is produced.

Since valid cognition depends upon the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the statement "at the time of its arising" (*utpattau*) is irrelevant. While the status of being an action and its factors (*kriyākārakatva*) was accepted with respect to the resulting cognition (*pramiti*), "arising" was not stated with respect to the state of being cognized (*avagamyamānatā*); however, in the case of knowledge (*jñāna*), even the state of being cognized [is relevant].

It is logical that [the cognition of the cloth] is dependent solely on its result. Furthermore, according to the doctrine of mere cognition (*jñānamātravāda*), there is a relationship of produced and producer only between cognitions and their latent impressions (*vāsanā*), not between one cognition and another cognition; therefore, even when the cognition of threads arises, the arising of the cognition of a cloth is not logically possible. Moreover, it is observed that there is a fixed cause when only the threads themselves are being employed.
The cloth is the condition; otherwise, even when there is no taking up of threads as material cause, the cognition of a cloth might occasionally arise for one whose sense faculties are unimpaired.

Therefore, this web of cognitions is not based solely on latent impressions (vāsanā). What then? It is established that it is based on real objects (artha). Consequently, the definition of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is justified.
“Inference is the cognition of an object not present to the senses, arising from the perception of one part [of a known relation] by one who knows that relation.
It is said, “by one who knows that relation”—of what is it the known relation? Surely, of one part.
This is not tenable, because the "one part" is subordinate to the act of perception; for a word that is subordinate cannot be construed with another word.

It is connected like "the king's man. Because neither the person nor the collection is mentioned, there is no connection. Therefore, we do not know—of what [subject] whose connection is known? It is said: this [objection] is based on a failure to understand the connection.

This is a delusion. But what is this relationship? This is the relationship: inference is the cognition of an object not present to the senses (*asannikṛṣṭa*) based on the perception of one part (*ekadeśa*). Based on the perception of which part?
Of that whose relationship [to the other] is known. But even in this case of relationship, the subordinate status of the "one part" remains exactly as it was.

The term "subordinate" (*upasarjana*) is not the cause for this relationship; likewise, the term "non-subordinate" (*anupasarjana*) is also not. That which is expected and capable of fulfilling that expectation attains the state of being related. And in this context, when it is said, "from the perception of one part," of what [part] is it?

There arises the expectation [of the word] *deśasya* (of the place), because perception has the visible object as its primary element, and because the cognition of another object is produced by that [perception].

For this very reason, it has been established in various instances that "in this case there is predominance of the second member" and "in this case there is predominance of the first member. Therefore, this designation of *upasarjana* (secondary member) is solely for the sake of establishing grammatical usage; [not for the sake of the meaning—]
For in the case of a relation, the cause is simply the mutual expectancy (*arthākāṅkṣā*) between meanings, not whether something is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) or not;
this is seen in such cases as "Whose teacher's family? (*kasya gurukulam*). It is said in reply: for what is pervaded (*vyāpya*) is observed to be... the pervader (*vyāpaka*).

He causes [it] to go; and as for the phrase "of one who knows the relation," this genitive case is not used in a pervasive sense; for they prescribe the genitive from a nominal stem that denotes merely a related entity. It is replied: True, the genitive refers to a related entity;

A related term (*sambandhin*) is indeed [only] that which is pervaded (*vyāpya*). For even in the case of an object that is not pervaded, the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs precisely when there is an intention to express it as being pervaded; we shall explain the meaning of the genitive in various such instances. And thus worldly people designate: "This is mine," or "But this belongs to another as well."
[Page 097] “That, however, is of two kinds.
What is this twofold nature? First, there is the twofold nature of its definition (lakṣaṇa).

[The inference] "it does not exist— because of the perception of a single part"— is [valid] because the definition [of the reason] is unitary. Now, if this is stated while accepting the twofold nature of the object of knowledge (*prameya*)—

namely, that in one case a particular is understood from a particular, and in another case the understanding of a universal arises from a universal— then by this distinction of the possessor of the reason (*hetumat*), a distinction in the reason (*hetu*) itself is also stated.

Furthermore, what is the purpose of stating the distinction between these two? By the statement of their definitions, their non-deviation (invariable concomitance) is established; and this effort is for that very purpose. Whether there be a twofold division of cause and effect or not, here certain people who consider themselves experts in logic [claim] that something whose specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not even determined can be known through inference.
They think that it is not apprehended in its general form; in order to dispel that misconception, this was stated: "But that is of two kinds."

Thus [it is said]: "Inference exists regarding actions and the like, which have as their object a particular (svalakṣaṇa) that is not perceived.
