But how can there be a perception of a related thing when the particular is not perceived? It has been stated: "Because of the perception of an effect that possesses an origin.

This has been established by us below in the discussion on the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*). Therefore, there exists an inference that results in a mere generality (*sāmānyamātra*). And it has been shown: "Devadatta’s [action] is preceded by motion"—and so forth. But what, then, is the...?

[Page 101] There is a deviation in the case of pride (*māna*), just as in the case of perception regarding mother-of-pearl and the like? But was this not just now demonstrated by the term "twofold"? Indeed, it is the non-inferential nature that must be refuted in what is not inferential, and not the inferential nature itself.

The definition must be stated. And what is the distinction here? For even those who accept both that which is inferential and that which is non-inferential still certainly allow for deviation in inference. Therefore, in this case as well, the purpose of stating the definition is precisely the exclusion of deviation. Furthermore, there would also be a confusion regarding the objects of knowledge (*prameya*). Not...
Some maintain that smoke seen in places such as kitchens is capable of establishing fire located on a mountain;
others hold that only particulars are understood; still others say it is merely a matter of memory. Therefore—[the word] "known" (jñāta)—is used.

"From the perception of one part of a relation, there arises the cognition of the other part which is not in contact"—thus [the author] qualifies [the definition]. What is excluded by this? First, memory is rejected by the phrase "which is not in contact.
Non-apprehension is also rejected by the mention of the "arising of cognition. This is because [cognition] arises from the comprehension of a relation.

Thus, even the apprehension of a specific distinction is refuted. Now, it might be argued that the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) cannot be asserted based merely on the arising of a cognition, because of the deviation seen in cases such as mother-of-pearl. Furthermore, the perception of something unrelated has already been answered by the very mention of [the requirement for] a relation. And when a relation is apprehended, a prior experience is unavoidable. Oh!
There is great negligence on the part of one who fails to distinguish between experience and recollection. Is it not possible for there to be an experience of what was previously seen?
Furthermore, experience is our means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Recollection is one thing, and experience is another. This is true.

Memory arises from the perception of a relation; however, with respect to another related object, there is indeed direct experience (*anubhava*). Therefore, logicians designate that which is perceived again and again as being close at hand—stating "it is indeed being seen"—and not "it is being remembered. Furthermore, it is established that inference and other means of knowledge consist of direct experience. Why?
In that case—what does "not in contact" mean?
It means being devoid of the conceit of recollection. [p. 104] sanni-...

For when there is a contact with what has been drawn forth [from memory], they consider that to be nothing other than recollection. But does this not result in its being equivalent to a lapse of memory (*smṛtipramoṣa*)?

No, because another cause, such as a logical mark (*liṅga*), is present; for in this case, the previous experience itself is not the cause. For in that case (of lapse), the cause of the error in memory is the lapse itself; here, however, the logical mark and so forth are present.

It is established that validity exists because there is a cause for it. Therefore, in this case as well, it must be stated that whatever is a means of valid cognition does not deviate; and this has already been said. This [principle] should also be applied to comparison (upamāna) and the other means of cognition.
[105] “The treatise is the cognition of an object not in contact [with the senses] arising from the cognition of words.
What is this "word"?

Regarding the phrase "from consciousness" (*vijñānāt*): does "consciousness of sound" (*śabdavijñāna*) mean consciousness arising from sound, or does it mean consciousness that has sound as its object? If it means consciousness that has sound as its object—that is, consciousness directed toward sound—then that is incorrect; for the teaching (*śāsana*) is not understood from that [sound]. Indeed, it is because of the teaching that there is a scripture (*śāstra*). Now, if [it refers to] sound...

The cognition that arises with respect to a particular object is the cognition of that word; in that regard, the cause for the apprehension of its specific distinction must be stated. And it has been said: "The treatise."

Thus [it is said]. For a treatise (*śāstra*) is so called because it instructs (*śāsana*); and that [instruction] is appropriate only in the case of a cognition whose object is the meaning (*artha*), not in the case of the word (*śabda*). Even in the second alternative, since it is established through its being the cause of that [cognition], it follows from the mention of "treatise. But is it not observed that there is also a semblance of a word (*śabdābhāsa*)?
“‘This son of a barren woman goes’—such statements and the like are also understood from the word itself;
for we do not perceive any other cause here, such as vapor or the like. This has already been answered: “If that [is the case]...”
Regarding the phrase "from a trustworthy person," this very fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is refuted by the statement of the definition.
“Comparison (upamāna) also produces a cognition regarding an object not present to the senses through similarity; for example, the sight of a gavaya [produces] the recollection of a cow.”

Thus: "similarity"—for this is what similarity is. "Of the recollection of the cow" means: of a person who has previously experienced the cow. But surely, the state of having a known relation is the same [in both cases], and that is the defining characteristic here.

In that case, what is the use of saying "either there or elsewhere"? It is certainly useful; for the definition given there is: "from the perception of one part," and "of one who knows the relationship."

This is the qualification. Therefore, the similarity residing in the gavaya is not a constituent part of the cognition of the similar [cow]. Furthermore, the cause of inference is that which has its relation observed repeatedly and which depends upon the exclusion from what is of a different class (*vijātīya-vyāvṛtti*); since neither of these two conditions exists here, it is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). What, then, is it?
Is it the observation of deviation that this definition is intended to exclude? Is there anything other than the appearance of similarity?
In this regard, some have stated that generality (*sāmānya*) itself is similarity; but that is not similarity. Why?
If so, it is indeed that very same [cognition], because the universal "cow-ness" and so forth are unitary. Now, some may think that in this case there is no object of knowledge (*prameya*) at all;
but that is incorrect, for it has been stated that even that which is experienced is an object of knowledge when it is understood through other causes.
Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is also the postulation of a fact because a perceived or heard fact cannot otherwise be accounted for—
just as, for example, by seeing the absence of the living Devadatta from his house, one infers his unperceived presence outside.
"conceptual construction.

What is this so-called "inexplicability otherwise"? If it means, first of all, that "its existence is not possible without this," then in that case, an inference of a cause from an effect has been proposed.
It is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). Now, it might be argued: "The definition of inference is 'that for which the relation is known' (*jñātasambandhasya*);

however, in this case, the relation is unknown; therefore, it is a separate means of valid cognition. This is incorrect. How can it be understood that the relation is unknown—namely, that "this [subject] is not possible without that [predicate]"?

The impossibility of an alternative explanation (*anyathānupapatti*) is not cognizable through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). For it is cognizable through the non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) of the effect;
and such non-deviation is preceded by repeated observation. Therefore, whether seen or unseen, it must be known—

The relationship itself is understood through the principle of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*). Therefore, [the claim that this is] another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is merely like a mirage.
True; if that which cannot be accounted for without something else were indeed the indicator of that thing, [then it would be a separate means of knowledge].

But here, it is precisely that which is not possible which is understood. And what is it that is not possible here? Since one observes the absence [of the person] from the house while he is alive, his absence elsewhere is not possible. What follows from this? That it is not the absence which is being cognized here.
Of what, then, is it the cognition? It is of existence; and that [existence] is not rendered possible by the observation of the absence from the house. Certainly, it is not possible.
[It] is inferred; for indeed, the existence [of someone] outside is not possible without seeing their absence from the house.
But is it not said: "An object seen or heard is not otherwise possible"?

Thus, he demonstrates that the indicator (*gamaka*) is otherwise inexplicable (*anyathānupapadyamānatā*). The "beloved of the gods" (*devānāṃ priyaḥ*) who does not understand the text asks: "Regarding the statement 'an object seen or heard leads to the postulation of another object' (*arthakalpanā*), what is this 'postulation of an object'? The meaning is that an object seen or heard serves as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for another object.

With what is the phrase “it is not otherwise possible” connected? We say it is connected with the means of valid cognition (*pramiti*); for it is by bringing about the impossibility of being otherwise that it leads to the understanding of another matter. Is it not the case here that the condition of having a known relation (*jñātasambandhitā*) is not required at all?

For it is the mere knowledge of the relation that is required, not the state of being related; however, in the case of inference, by the genitive case in the phrase "of one who has known the relation," it is stated that the state of being related itself is the means of comprehension.
The mention of "seen or heard" is for the purpose of introducing another cause.

"To a slave? We say "no"; the meaning is that the object has been apprehended. Now, for what purpose is the mention of "heard" (śruta)? One might simply say "seen" (dṛṣṭa). It is replied: this is indeed a different designation—
"Seen or heard" is a designation for perception.
“Non-existence, too, is the absence of a means of valid cognition [regarding] the object ‘it does not exist,’ which is not in contact [with the senses].”

"Non-existence, too, is the absence of a means of valid cognition"—is this the definition of a means of valid cognition? Yes—it is so stated. What is cognized by this? It has been said: the meaning is "it does not exist."

Furthermore, what is it that does not exist? It is the state of being an object of cognition (*prameyatā*) for that which is currently being cognized (*pramīyamāṇa*); and thus, the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*) for that which is not yet cognized (*apramiti*) appears almost as something contrary to worldly experience. Even its definition—"the absence of a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇābhāva*)—is likewise problematic.

Thus, it characterizes [the opponent's position] as not being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, there is this well-known tradition among the Mīmāṃsakas: "This is indeed a sixth means of knowledge. And neither from the text nor from common worldly usage...

[Page 121] Validity is thus determined. Therefore, we do not know what the seed of this well-known status is. What is it that is not known here? First of all, from the text itself, the very absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is determined; namely, "it does not exist."

Even when this is stated, worldly people understand the non-existence of the object of cognition (*prameya*). What, then, is the purpose of defining it? This undertaking is for the sake of understanding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for how else could the determination of an object follow from that? Therefore—

This is what is being said: since this undertaking has the purpose of understanding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is it by this [work] that the nature of the previously mentioned means of valid cognition is determined? [The answer is: No, for that which was not determined by the previously stated specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) [is not determined here]. This entire treatise is a supplement to the statements defining all specific characteristics; for it is not from the mere arising of a cognition that its object is known.

The validity of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is ascertained; therefore, because all means of valid cognition are understood through their nature as ascertainment due to the expression of the mere particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), for that reason:
Because the effect has ceased to exist, it is said that "it does not exist"; by this, the validity of the previously stated definition itself is affirmed.

What, then, is this "common consensus" (*prasiddhi*)? It is a consensus like that of the "yakṣa in the banyan tree. If, however, you think there is a difference in the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because there is a difference in linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), what can we do? For a difference in linguistic usage does not establish a difference in the means of valid cognition. Therefore, this is indeed its definition; and this alone is its definition. Consequently:
The causal sign (nimitta) need not be examined because it is already well-established.

[124] "Granted that perception and the other means of knowledge may indeed exist; however, verbal testimony (*śabda*) is not a means of knowledge. Why? Because it is not a cause [of knowledge], since it apprehends only what is already present. It is not a cause.

"Verbal testimony is not a valid means of knowledge; for that which is not perceived despite being within the range of perception does not exist, just as the horn of a hare. And the senses are the instruments of perception for animals and the like.
Yet, animals are not perceived immediately after the sacrifice performed by one desiring cattle. Therefore, this sacrifice does not have cattle as its fruit."

Let perception and the other means of knowledge be valid; however, what is the intention behind the claim that verbal testimony (*śabda*) is not a valid means of knowledge? This is the intention: as for what was stated regarding its "independence" (*anapekṣatva*), it refers to [the independence of] the means of knowledge...

To say that it makes known an object not previously understood is merely false. Why? Because its status as a means of valid cognition was stated on the grounds that "this object is yet to come," being something to be realized; that [status] is not possible here.

But how is it impossible? Is there such a thing as a sentence devoid of an injunction (*niyoga*)? What would an injunction accomplish in this case? For we observe that [injunctions] apply even to matters already understood through other means of knowledge, as in the case of the *smṛtis* and so forth. Therefore, having considered only that object which is understood through application (*viniyoga*), the scope of the injunction must be stated. And this very application—
In cases such as "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā," that which is perceived is indeed an object already existing at the time of perception.

What here is meant by "perception of what is present"? It is the state of having the fruit [of the action] immediately following the performance of the act. Furthermore, because rain and such have visible results, it can be said that they are actually cognizable through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) due to their state of having immediate fruits.
And since they are capable of being objects of other means of knowledge, who indeed would claim that the word possesses independence regarding the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) in the world?
Is it possible to conceive [of it otherwise]? Therefore, it must be understood that *niyoga* (an injunction) has precisely the meaning of a command (*praiṣa*) and so forth.
This is the answer to the question "From where?"—namely, "Because it is the apprehension of what is already existent."
This is the reply.
But if the text is explained in this way, then the passage beginning with "animals are not perceived" would be meaningless.
Whether animals are perceived or not, the point to be established here is simply this: that verbal cognition is dependent upon other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This much is indeed what is to be established; and who has said that anything else is to be established?

It was stated that the presentation of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is not tenable. This is not so; it is indeed tenable. The purpose of this passage is to state that validity must be asserted through the examination of another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*), and not intrinsically (*svataḥ*). And that other means of knowledge is seen here. But how is there an understanding of what is seen here? Because the result occurs immediately after the activity.

How then is it with agriculture and the like? Is no fruit perceived immediately following agriculture and so forth? Is it that the fruit of the action (*kriyā-phala*) is not understood, or rather the fruit of the purpose (*prayojana-phala*)? First, the cutting up of the parts of the earth is the fruit of the action.

It is not understood [as the primary purpose]; rather, the production of rice (*vrīhi*) is the instrumental result (*prayojanaphala*). Nor is it called "unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*) due to the lack of understanding of a purpose;

for in this case, the purpose and the fruit are understood to be the cattle themselves, since no other fruit is perceived. And whatever modification of the oblation (*havirvikāra*) is perceived, that—unlike the splitting [of the grain] and so forth—is not a cause of cattle for the production of rice and the like.

It can be argued that [the Veda] cannot be a source of knowledge because it is not perceived; therefore, those who desire to know Dharma must investigate other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), and not derive an understanding of Dharma from the mere study [of the Veda]. But how [is this so] in the case of [injunctions such as] "one who desires heaven" and so forth?

Who is it that, upon the employment and the verbal expression of this [word], determines the conceptual cognition associated with its employment regarding the object denoted? To exclude such a notion, he stated:
"The form (ākṛti) qualified by the dewlap and so forth. And this is mentioned for the sake of illustration, just like the mention of the verbal expression itself.
“Is it not the case that the universal (ākṛti) either exists or does not exist as the object to be proven?”—
thus, by virtue of being denotable, it possesses the nature of a word.
He stated that [the nature] does not abandon [its own form]. Now, one might ask: what is the purpose of designating it as "non-existent" when it has attained that very form?

This "non-existence" was stated with reference to its status as a denotable object (*abhidheya*), not with reference to its intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*). For it cannot be something to be proven (*sādhya*) while being perceptible (*pratyakṣa*).
—thus it is said. If, at most, the non-existence of the very nature [of the object] were being proven, then indeed there would be inexpressibility;
however, non-existence cannot be asserted, because [the object] is accessible through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). "If you say it is a delusion," [it is replied:

Thus [it was asked]. And by whom was it said that "its non-existence is by its very nature"? But the other, having taken that very intention to heart, said: "There is no delusion when there is no subversion of cognition. "Even though it does not exist—"
If it is argued that such a cognition arises with respect to a different object, as in the case of [the words] ‘a row,’ ‘a herd,’ or ‘a forest.’”

—Thus, he reveals the non-existence [of the universal] by way of its being denotable. This matter being stated is not at all contradicted by perception, namely, the non-existence of the configuration (ākṛti). What then? It is the non-existence of the form of the denoter as having the nature of the denoted.

"It is understood"—thus it was stated; and this is not tenable for one who maintains the theory of non-transformation (*avivarta-vādin*). Therefore, the intention is that the position of illusory transformation (*vivarta-pakṣa*) alone is superior. [This applies] even to the passage beginning with "this statement presented is incoherent" (*asambaddham idaṃ vacanam upanyastam*).

The intended meaning is that there is no cognition of the form of the word at all. How, then, can there be a single cognition? For in cases such as a "row" (*paṅkti*), nothing else is perceived as a single entity distinct from the two words; yet this single cognition does exist.
Therefore, it is based solely upon the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the word. [As it is said: "Is there a cognition of a forest when no forest exists?"

Thus, if there were no single entity denoted by the word "forest" distinct from the trees, the cognition of "one" would not be possible; can it then be said that even the trees themselves, which are apprehended through direct perception, do not exist? What is the intention [behind this question]?
In this case, it is only the trees that are perceived as a unity; the nature of the word "forest" is not apprehended. Now, if the intention is this—"even the trees do not exist"—then...

"For even that form is merely superimposed upon the word"—thus is the Mahāyāna position refuted. For it has been stated that perceptual consciousness has the external object as its domain, not the cognition itself. Even if consciousness were to have cognition as its object, how would that establish the superimposition of the word?

For the cognition of individual trees is one thing, and the cognition of a forest is another. Therefore, whether it has as its object the mental construction (*buddhi*) or the external entity (*artha*), one must simply state that in either case the nature of the word "forest" does not exist [in the objects themselves]. Consequently, it is perception itself that is being challenged here.
The preceding passage appears to be entirely incoherent. Therefore, it seems that the very existence of the universal (ākṛti) is being challenged.
This is not so; for those who maintain that the word "forest" possesses a [single] form, the answer is simply the cognition of distinct forms. That...

And here, it is perceived as distinct from the form of the tree; at most, there would be a non-perception due to its absence, but that absence is not tenable when perception stands as the adversary. Now, it may be argued that "cognition is perception" is indeed tenable.
Thus it has been said. No, for the cognition of difference is biased toward conceptual construction (*parikalpanā*). Therefore, it is well stated:
"That Mahāyāna position has been refuted.
[Objection: But surely this single cognition is entirely without an objective support (*anālambana*)?

[This objection] has been reached: "Now, why is it that you are being censured for having a nature consisting of a form— namely, that 'your other established doctrine is flawed, for even when a forest does not exist, the cognition of a forest would follow'?"
What, then, is the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) here that is being refuted? It is this: "The singular number [is used] after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) denoting a single entity.
And yet, there are many trees; and you, long-lived one, have stated that this [word *vṛkṣāḥ*] is a nominal stem. Just as the generic form (*ākṛti*) exists—

Thus, this case is exactly like that. This constitutes a refutation of the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*). If there is a refutation because the Smṛti is rooted in another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), let it be so; for one cannot declare something to be faulty simply on the grounds of a refutation of its own acceptance. This reason—namely, "cognition through direct perception" (*pratyakṣāvagati*)—is not faulty. Therefore, if—
Even in the absence of singularity, there is the singular number; what can we do? Whom shall we blame? This is not an object for reproach.
The rule that "the singular number is used for a single thing" is merely a general tendency (*prāyika*), as it is seen to deviate in cases such as *dāra* (wife/wives).

Because of the usage; this singular number is functional (*prāyaugika*), not inherent (*ānvayika*). Therefore, it is only a lack of understanding of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that is to be censured here. Consequently, it is established that in no case is there a cognition superimposed upon a word; thus [the view of] Jaimini is proven.

Nervaca [states]: "The meaning of a word is the form (ākṛti). He will demonstrate more thoroughly in the section on Form (Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa) that words such as "cow" function as causes of cognition by means of the apprehension of the form.
"Now, what is this 'relation' (sambandha)? It is that by which, when the word is understood, the meaning is understood.
But what is this relation that is both questioned and proposed? We reply: it is precisely that which was mentioned previously. [Objection: But is not that...
The relationship is characterized by the name and the named; therefore, one might think that this relationship is something entirely distinct [from the two]. That is incorrect;
for even in that case, there is the relationship between the signified and the signifier characterized by the name and the named.

Thus, this very relationship characterized by the signified (*jñāpya*) and the signifier (*jñāpaka*) has been described. Now, [one might ask]: "Is it not the case that the relationship between the signified and the signifier is characterized as that between the name (*saṃjñā*) and the named (*saṃjñin*)?"

By saying this—specifically by the use of the genitive case in the expression "of the signified" (*pratyāyyasya*) and "of the signifier" (*pratyāyakasya*)—another kind of relation is expressed. This is not so;
rather, it is precisely this relationship of signifier and signified that is presented by the genitive as being characterized by the nature of name (*saṃjñā*) and named (*saṃjñin*). Why is this?
But does not the genitive case express distinction (*vyatireka*)? Indeed, there is here a distinction by way of the relation of cause and effect;

the relationship characterized as that between a name and the named is the basis for expressing the state of being the signifier and the signified. Otherwise, the mention of the signified and the signifier would be purposeless. Yet you do not point out that single [relation] which—

It should be stated that this concerns the characteristic of the designation and the designated. For this very reason, by means of the passage, “But that is produced, as has been established previously,” he makes it clear that this is a restatement of what was already said before. What, then, is the reason?

Regarding the *Praśna* and *Upanyāsa*: the reason here is this—the question arises for one who thinks that, in the case of a superimposition (*vivarta*), it is impossible to assert the independence of two things established separately (*yutasiddha*). [The answer is: It is possible, because the usage of the elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*) is beginningless.
[Page 177]
In order to state that [the Veda] is independent [of an author], he introduces that very point: "But it is produced.
This was said with the same intention as previously described: "Therefore, we consider that by some person [the connection] of words with their meanings..."

"The Vedas were composed for the purpose of worldly transaction after establishing the relationship [between word and meaning]"—thus was their dependence [on human agency] concluded. "Now, this is stated: 'Because the relationship is not of human origin, it is established.'"
This is an introduction to the statement regarding the beginninglessness of traditional usage (*vṛddhavyavahāra*). What, then, is this question and answer?
When asked "How?", [the answer is] "Because of the absence of a person who could relate [it]."
—this reply is inappropriate.
This has been set forth in order to refute the counter-argument regarding the beginninglessness of the linguistic usage of the elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*). But how is this so?

Is it suspected [that the relationship] is due to its being a counteragent? Indeed, it is so suspected; for even though the comprehension of meaning from a word is established through beginningless usage by the elders (*vṛddha*), where an author is perceived, there the very fact of having a beginning follows by the force of that perception, as in the case of "vṛddhir ādaic."
...as [in the previous case]. Therefore, the perception of an agent must be refuted. To the question, "How is it that there is no connection?"—does this answer, "Of perception... [hold up]?

"Because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and because the others are preceded by it"—how is this not tenable? For even inference and the other [means] are admitted to be means of valid cognition. Furthermore, being "preceded by that" is incorrect, since verbal testimony (*śabda*) is dependent...

Because it would follow that [the word] is perishable, and because it would result in actions and so forth not being inferable; furthermore, if the word were dependent [on something else], the effort to establish its innate nature (*autpattikatva*) would be entirely futile. Thus, this situation has arisen: "The horseman has forgotten the horse upon which he is mounted."

This objection arises from a failure to understand the underlying intention: namely, that it is impossible for [the object] to be cognizable solely through inference or scripture when the beginningless linguistic usage of elders stands as an adversary. Therefore, perception is primary, and scripture and inference are preceded by it.
"It is not to be refuted. Therefore, the response is logically established. Now, for what purpose is the plural number used in "of the others"?
It should rather have been said as "of the two," since only two are presented as being subject to doubt. Of the two—
The presentation of what is to be suspected [is as follows]: "But the impossibility of all [of them]" justifies the use of the plural number.
[The opponent] states that [the reason] "because they occurred long ago" is unestablished (*asiddha*). How is it unestablished? [Because it refers to] the ancestors...

Because it is possible for [the object] to be within the scope of direct perception. The phrase "for what has long since passed away would not fail to be remembered" implies that direct perception of the ancestors is not possible here;
if such perception were indeed possible, they would be remembered just as Pāṇini is.
“Furthermore, non-remembrance [of the Veda] cannot be like that of wells, groves, and so forth, in places such as the Himavat mountains.
Regarding that non-remembrance:

A cause such as separation from a person (puruṣa-viyoga) is possible; yet there is no separation from a person for words—what is intended by this? For if they were of the class of produced things (kṛtaka), their validity would follow from that [person's] validity.

The intention is that the interruption of memory cannot be justified by its being purposeless. And this has been demonstrated by the citation of Pāṇini and Piṅgala: "Even if forgetting were possible, nevertheless we could not establish an author of the relationship without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); just as one does not perceive something that exists [without a means of perception]."
"We would not accept the existence of a hare's horn on this basis alone without a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
And even if forgetfulness were possible,"

Thus, what is the object of this instance of forgetfulness that has been put forward? If it refers to the object of the probandum, then this itself is the proof—namely, the occurrence of forgetfulness. And it has been said:

Regarding the statement, "forgetting is possible"— then the claim that "we do not apprehend a creator of the relationship without a means of valid cognition" is not a valid reason. Furthermore, as for what is said, "there may be non-perception even of something that exists," it does not follow from this alone [that such a creator does not exist].
"Without a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), we apprehend a rabbit's horn"—
this too is incorrect; for if it were only that which exists which is not perceived, who could say— "the rabbit's horn..."?

"Do we not experience [this], saying 'the horn of a hare does not exist'? Now, if your intention is this—that although the possibility of forgetfulness is observed elsewhere, one cannot on that account assert the possibility of forgetfulness in this case as well—this is an incorrect intention; for it is certainly said that what is observed in one place occurs in another."

For this indeed is the domain of the inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*). To this it is replied: neither forgetfulness nor non-perception is being presented here as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); rather, it is the defect of the cause regarding an object that has been perceived.

This is presented for the purpose of refutation. However, it has been stated that this [argument] is irrelevant because you have presented it here as a case of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) alone. Just as the non-apprehension of an apprehended object such as a jar exists, one cannot on that basis assert the existence of a rabbit's horn. Non-apprehension of an object within the scope of apprehension is due to other causes...
It does not depend on anything else; however, when there is non-apprehension, the non-apprehension of that non-apprehension follows from non-apprehension itself. Therefore, this is well said:
"But surely, by presumptive testimony (arthāpatti)..."
Thus, why has this designation "means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa) been introduced? It is replied: "Yes. But what, then, is grasped here by this thought, "it is not tenable"?

[Objection: But surely there is an author of the relationship [between word and meaning]. [Question: How, then, is that [author] not tenable? [Answer: Because the meaning is not understood upon the first hearing. [Objection: If one does not comprehend the meaning upon the first hearing, what follows regarding the author of the relationship? [Response: In that case, if Devadatta is not perceived in the house, what follows?
Regarding external existence? We do not say that external existence is untenable. What then? It was stated that its actual presence is untenable. This very thing—[it] exists externally [p.

—Thus [ends the discussion on] consciousness. But here, since the meaning is not understood upon the first hearing, what kind of relation between [the word and its meaning] has been observed by the author? Or perhaps this occurs to the mind: "People do not comprehend [the meaning] from the first hearing, yet they do comprehend it upon the second hearing and so forth; therefore, some other cause besides the word must be sought."
[Question: Is this then an inference from an effect (*kārya*) that has been presented as an inference from a cause (*kāraṇa*)? [Answer: How then is it said to be "by implication" (*arthāpattyā*)?
The meaning is: the occurrence of an inference from the fact (*artha*). Why? Because it was stated: "from the fact which is the effect. But is this not an inference?

Even this is not tenable, because it is not understood upon the first hearing and because it is inconclusive, since understanding arises from the Vedic sentence itself when heard for the first time. But surely this inquiry concerns the word (*pada*). What, then, is this thing called a "word"? It is "cow" and so forth.

In sentences such as "Devadatta, bring the cow," are [the words] well-known as having distinct objects to be accomplished (*kārya*), or is the comprehension of the sentence-meaning itself the object to be accomplished? Certainly, they are well-known as having distinct objects to be accomplished. In what context? In linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). By means of what do elders engage in usage? [By means of sentences such as: "Devadatta, bring the white cow."
—by such statements as these.
If that is so, then linguistic usage proceeds by means of the sentence-meaning; for indeed, no object is established through linguistic usage that is not [already] well-known.

It can be understood through its distinct function. How then [is this so]? For even when there is no [external object], there is the answer: "Now, what is the meaning of this word 'cow'? It is the generic form (*ākṛti*) characterized by the dewlap and so forth."
If there were a difference in the effect (*kārya*), how could its innate nature (*autpattikatva*) be asserted on the basis of the usage of elders?
Therefore, this text must be explained in such a way that the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the proof (*sādhana*) form a single coherent statement.
That [explanation], however, is provided by the Commentator himself in the section concerning "that which has become that" (*tadbhūta-adhikaraṇa*); thus, we shall desist here.

[189] What, then, is the resolution of the inconclusiveness? That is stated with the intention of referring to the cause (*nimitta*): one who has not apprehended the cause does not understand from the mere first hearing. Therefore, the intention is that there exists another cause distinct from the word itself.

What, then, is the difference between the denoter (*vācaka*) and the cause (*nimitta*)? It is precisely for this purpose that the section beginning with "That which has come into being" (*tadbhūtādhikaraṇa*) is commenced; enough of this prolixity. [The Sūtra says: "No, because the instruction is given as if it were already established" (*na, siddhavadupadeśāt*). What does this mean—"as if it were already established"?

Regarding the objection "How so?"—this is the response: here, no agent can be postulated, because the linguistic usage of the elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*) is beginningless; therefore, it is established that the relationship is innate (*autpattika*).

[Page 192] What is this? It has been introduced in one way and concluded in another: it was introduced with the claim that "the comprehension of meaning arises from the word alone," yet it is concluded with "from the linguistic usage of elders. This is like placing a burden elsewhere—

It falls elsewhere, like a cluster of arrows from an unskilled archer. Even when a meaning is understood through the usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*), the meaning is not understood from the word itself, as in the case of hand gestures and the like.
Hand gestures and such are also established solely through the usage of elders; they are not inherently connected to the meaning.
For it is linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) alone that is the cause for the comprehension of meaning, not hand gestures and the like; these are merely conditions (*upādhi*) for proficiency.

Therefore, the word is an auxiliary condition (*upādhi*), not the direct cause of the understanding of meaning, just as the whip, the goad, and the strike of a lance are [not the causes of movement itself].

For this very reason, it has been said by those who know the nature of sound: "The proponents of the Veda must resort to the theory of illusory manifestation (vivarta) alone. To this, we reply: what is the use of this partiality for the theory of illusory manifestation? This [position] has already been refuted due to the non-perception of oneness. If it is thus refuted, then the authority of the Veda remains intact.

To this it is replied: When the meaning is being understood through the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*), what other cause for that understanding do you consider it to be besides the word? Surely, you consider linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) itself to be the cause.
Not so; for linguistic proficiency concerns the relationship between word and meaning; it is not the case that the word and its meaning [arise] from proficiency.

[The relation] is the usage; for it is only linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*) that has a beginning, but not the relationship between word and meaning, because that [relationship] is its object. Therefore: "No; because the instruction is given as something already established."
Well said!
But even if the relationship is one of cause and effect, is it not still the case that the understanding of elders' usage is entirely conducive to the learning of children?

How is this presented as an opposing argument? It is true; for when an effect is to be known through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no contradiction in the process of linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*), just as there is none in the derivation from grammar and so forth—provided it concerns something that is to be inferred (*kalpya*).
Furthermore, it precludes conceptual construction; and it has already been stated that there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for this.
Moreover, if the relationship were something produced, there would be no purpose whatsoever in a creator establishing that relationship in places difficult of access.

There is a purpose [for this]: for the establishment of a relationship is indeed for the sake of practical usage (*saṃvyavahāra*), and practical usage is not possible for those situated in inaccessible places. Furthermore, a relationship that is an effect (*kārya*) is not possible without words that denote the relata (*sambandhin*).
If it is accepted that the relationship exists for the sake of an effect, then the effect is already accomplished. But is it not the case that there is also linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*)?

[Page 197] It indeed depends upon its being an effect. How so? For one who does not know that "this is the designator of this [object]," comprehension from the word is not possible. Indeed, there is nothing that is impossible when it is observed; for [the relationship] arises simply from linguistic usage.
The understanding of the ignorant is observed [to be otherwise]. Therefore, when a matter is established by direct perception in this manner, it is not reasonable to postulate an agent.
Furthermore, this [postulation] is useless for practical activity; for if the relationship were something produced, then that which is unobservable—

The establishment of a relationship between a mental object, such as a deity, and its corresponding word is impossible; indeed, it has been described as being incapable. Therefore, because the relationship is innate (*autpattika*), its independence is established.

"Now, as for what was said—'the word is without cause'—why is this objection raised? This has already been answered by the statement that the relationship [between word and meaning] is innate (autpattika). Of what [is it without cause]?"

Is the refutation of another [position] understood through the statement regarding its innate nature (*autpattikatva*)? No other [point] has been introduced; for it is precisely by virtue of being perceived as something presently existing that the absence of any other object for the injunction (*niyoga*) is established.
It has been shown in such passages as, "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā [offering].
True, this very [objection] was stated as a rebuttal to the claim that the relationship is innate (*autpattika*); however, even if the relationship were innate...
The distinction from other objects appears as if it has not yet been stated; this is presented again for the sake of that distinction:
"Because the fruit is not seen at the time of the action, and because the action no longer exists at a later time.
But surely, by this—

What is it? It has been shown that because there is no other object, and because it is dependent on being the object of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it lacks validity in the absence of that [other object]; here too, it is the same. But what, then, is that?

Does it not seem as though something has been left unsaid? This is it: for when there is an object within the scope of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), an injunction (*niyoga*) takes the form "by this [means], this [result] [is to be achieved]. In that case, if the object is not perceived, its lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) is quite evident.
Furthermore, it is not possible in this matter that the fulfillment of the injunction arises from the injunction itself.
It might be possible to imagine this; however, that [imagined position] is now refuted: this might be so, if there were no inherent nature (autpattikatā);
yet that has been established. What follows from this? This follows from it: [p. 201]

The injunction does not depend upon this meaning, namely "by this [means] this [end is achieved]"; for even in the case of a worldly matter cognizable through other means of knowledge, no dependence on the establishment of the relationship between the means and the end is observed for the injunction. [This is so even when there is] a defect in the cause—
It is refuted in order to dispel misconceptions, but not with regard to self-awareness. Therefore, "the independence of the injunction" [is established].

By this, discrimination (*viveka*) is demonstrated. For, as he will establish in the sixth [chapter], that which enjoins a person makes known the accomplishment of what is to be achieved (*sādhyasiddhi*). If this is so, is non-perception of the immediate (*anantarānupalabdhi*) thereby refuted? Certainly it is refuted; for in this view, [the proof] does not proceed from the determination of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*).

The accomplishment of the goal [is not established by the word itself]. What then? It is by virtue of the force of the injunction (*niyoga*). Consequently, only this much is understood: "From this, its accomplishment [occurs]," but not whether it occurs immediately or after an interval.
Thus [it is said]. And that independence has been established from various perspectives. What is this [statement]: "If there were only five means of valid cognition"?
This very thing [is what is meant]. But was it not already stated: "Non-existence, too, is the absence of a means of valid cognition"?
Thus [it is asked]: what follows if this is so? This follows from it: that there are five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not tenable.

Or can it be said that [the non-existence of a thing] does not exist by means of four [means]? Then non-existence (*abhāva*) is a means of valid cognition; or rather, [is it not] a means of valid cognition?

Can it be said that there is an absence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*)? Since non-existence (*abhāva*) possesses the status of a means of valid cognition, it depends upon objects such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth with respect to its object. Therefore, this [non-existence] functions solely by delimiting an object already cognized through another means of valid cognition.

The definition has been stated. However, the difference in conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is already established. This presentation is for the sake of establishing conventional usage, not for the sake of establishing the essential nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). What fault is there in accepting another means of valid cognition?
Indeed, there is no fault whatsoever; however, it would simply mean that what is not a means of valid cognition is called a means of valid cognition.
Furthermore, the *Lakṣaṇa* treatise would be disregarded, and the independence of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would be refuted.
Therefore, it is established that the word has a distinct object; and once that is established, its status as a valid means of knowledge is also established.

For what purpose, then, is the mention of "five" made? It is for the sake of demonstrating the fivefold nature of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). For if the mention of "five" were not made, another form of linguistic usage would not be demonstrated. Therefore, they consider the linguistic usage expressed as "the branch is fruitless" to be based solely on perception. And this linguistic usage arises from the delimitation of the object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, it cannot be said that the delimitation of the objects of the means of valid cognition constitutes a separate object; nor does the mere comprehension of the object itself constitute the delimitation of the previous means of valid cognition. Thus, it is not the case that [the means of valid cognition] do not exist.
Thus, conventional usage is rendered possible. Therefore, it is established that there is a difference from conventional usage. For this very reason, regarding conventional usage— [p.
The presentation of the number five pertains only to time; it is not at the time of stating the nature of the means of valid cognition that the number six is presented.

Therefore, since the number five is presented precisely here, you should understand this: this number five is a differentiator for the conventional usage of non-existence (*abhāva*), not for its essential nature (*svarūpa*). As for the [objection regarding] common consensus, an answer has already been given.
As for the statement that was put forward as being contradicted by perception— namely, “This very sacrificer, equipped with the sacrificial implements, goes directly to the heavenly world”—
it designates the perceptible body [as the sacrificer].
Thus, even here, it is unestablished that [the Self] is the "body" (śarīraka). Who, then, is designated by this term? It is he to whom this body belongs. But is it not said, "this one"?
Thus is the designation, not "of whom this [is the body]," because it is a metaphorical treatment of non-difference (*abhedopacāra*).

This designation is based on a connection—just as in the expression, "The platforms cry out. Why is the figurative meaning of a word accepted? Because such is the understanding [derived from it]; for it has been stated that since the words of an *arthavāda* (explanatory passage) have another purpose, their comprehension is indeed figurative (*gauṇī*).
But surely, a figurative reference occurs only when there is a perception of difference between the two, as in the case of the cow and the Vāhīka?
The statement "the Vāhīka is an ox" is thus established;
yet we do not perceive anything here other than the body. What is the intention behind saying "we do not perceive"? This is precisely the intention: we do not perceive [anything else].

Thus [it is said]. But surely we perceive [the self] through the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth, which are effects; surely it is the body itself that breathes in and breathes out? What do you mean by "body," long-lived one? Is it this which is composed of the four elements?

[The term] *saṅghāta* [is used]. For these are not effects of the body, because they do not persist as long as the body exists; that is to say, because they do not persist as long as the primary elements (*bhūta*) exist. Even though they possess the nature of being derived from the primary elements, they are not perceived like visible form (*rūpa*) and so forth in the case of those [elements] that are not appropriated.

Furthermore, it cannot be maintained that pleasure and the like are properties of the primary elements (*bhūtadharma*); for the properties of the primary elements, such as form and so forth, are perceivable by other sense-faculties just like the primary elements themselves, whereas pleasure and the like are not. Let it be granted that pleasure and the like are not properties of the primary elements;
however, what proof is there for something else distinct from them? Is it not the case that this [pleasure] is an effect, and an effect does not exist without a cause?

"It is not tenable"—this alone is the proof in this matter. Furthermore, since the inherent causality (*samavāyi-kāraṇatā*) of the elements has been refuted, it is established that [sound] is a property of something else. This is not established, because they are mutually effects of one another.
Because [the objection] is not tenable. As for what was said— that "it cannot be asserted that whatever is perceived must necessarily have a correlate"—
that appears to be incorrect.

How can that which is observed to possess an origin not lead to the understanding of another related factor? For it is established that an origin must have a cause. This statement refers to a dissimilar cause; it does not mean, however, that an origin is said to be without a cause at all.
But how is it understood that this refers to a dissimilar cause? "For indeed... [the text continues].
In the passage “[the moon or the sun],” the term refers to “another related entity.”

This is because of the hearing of the word "antara" (intermediate). Now, one might object that the word "antara" is indeed applicable even when there is difference; this is true, it is applicable, but it cannot be understood that "the effect is not the cause. Let it be so.
The flaw lies in the composition of the text; however, a fault is not itself the cause for understanding a different meaning. No, because a continuum (*santāna*) is admitted;
for a continuum is based on the relationship between cause and effect. Therefore, [it is not] dissimilar—
[215] Understand that this is intended as a reason (*hetu*). Therefore, this web of effects has precisely a homogeneous continuum (*sabhāga-santati*) as its cause;
there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for perceiving anything dissimilar here—thus it is concluded. And if...

Without a dissimilar [cause], there would be no arising, and there would be a lack of regularity. By this very reasoning, the notions of "agent" and "word-meaning" are refuted, as well as desire and memory, because nothing else is observed;
for it cannot be said that memory and the rest are impossible unless another dissimilar [cause] is observed.
For indeed, there is nothing that is impossible regarding what is perceived. Thus it has been said: "Where do we have any conviction that something is impossible?"

Thus [it is asked]: what, then, is the reason that all these causes for the cognition of a self are presented and then refuted by the author of the Commentary? It is because through these, the notion of a self arises with respect to what is not the self;
and ignorance must be eliminated in every possible form. But how do these causes lead to the notion of a self in what is not the self?
[Page 217] How do they produce [this cognition]? As for what was stated— “We perceive this [self] by means of the vital breaths and so forth”—
it is as follows:

What is unreasonable here? These [qualities] are not properties of the elements (*bhūta*), because they do not exist as long as the elements exist and because they are not observed in jars and the like. Once their status as elemental properties has been refuted, and since it is understood that they must belong to something else by virtue of being dependent, they are the qualities of the self (*ātman*), because the mind (*citta*) and its objects (*cetya*) are themselves dependent [upon it].
Thus, it was rightly said: "For these [are non-self]. How can it be asserted that by means of this [body], the cognition of a self regarding what is not-self is possible?
For pleasure and so forth, being perceived as dependent [on the body], do not exist for as long as the elements exist.

And these have been correctly described as qualities of the self. To this it is replied: first of all, prāṇa and the others cannot be said to exist as long as the elements exist, because they are of the nature of motion; for this is the characteristic of wind, and in all instances such as breathing and so forth, only the nature of motion is perceived. Therefore, [the claim that they] exist as long as the elements exist—

This is well known: this is the notion of a self in what is not-self. As for pleasure and the other qualities that were proposed, they too can be said to be merely qualities of the primary elements (*bhūta*), because they are caused by the transformation of those elements; for a quality-less entity is not capable of transforming a possessor of qualities. Indeed, transformation is a state (*avasthā*); and a state belongs to the possessor of the state as a different state [of that same entity].

[This is] the cause for its arising; and since the state is not distinct from that which possesses the state, it is established that [pleasure and so forth] are qualities of the primary elements (*bhūta*). But surely, this very point should have been stated [earlier]. Why was it said: "Granted, pleasure and so forth might be thus"?

The intention is that even if this point were conceded, it would not be established, because of the mention of "desire" (kāma). What, then, is the reason for conceding this? This is the reason: here there are certain people who possess pride in their own wisdom.
Those who hold contrary views ask: "What is this so-called relationship of support and supported? Only a mere aggregate is perceived here;

for the relationship of support and supported does not exist among the elements (bhūtas) themselves when they are perceived together. Therefore, it has been demonstrated that those [factors] such as pleasure and the rest must either be independent or [must have] a support. Thus it is accepted.

On this point, other knowers of Brahman have reached the conclusion: "Because of the mention of an agent in the Smṛti and because of [the existence of] desire, we perceive the Self as distinct from the body, which begins with the Mahat and ends with the elements. How so?

Is it because of their repeated assertions and other reasons that [the self] is said to be the cause? For the internal organ, such as the *mahat* and so forth, consists of cognition, and the object of knowledge is its effect;
therefore, one can say that "it knows" as something distinct from both the effect and the instrument.
For there is the conviction that one should contemplate something by means of knowledge; therefore, the self is established as the agent.
Now, it has been stated that this [self] is inactive; for [the suffix] in the verb "he knows" (jānāti) denotes the agent of the cognition.

Thus, this is the condition (*pratyaya*). For those [schools] for whom cognition inheres in the self (*ātman*), its status as the agent of the condition is established precisely because it is the cause thereof. Furthermore, for those for whom cognition and the other qualities are well-known solely as attributes of the intellect (*buddhi*), this [self] is the cause by virtue of being the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*). How is it said that perception arises from desire? It is stated as follows:

For desire (*abhilāṣa*) is a longing for an object previously experienced; and such a conceit of having previously experienced something is not tenable in regard to the momentary aggregates (*skandha*). But surely, there is nothing that is impossible regarding what is perceived. Indeed, there is no impossibility in what is perceived, but rather— [p.

It cannot be said that the alteration of what has been seen is impossible because it was seen; for this is precisely the alteration of what was seen. Therefore, it has been stated that we perceive another [agent] who performs actions by will.

Likewise, from memory; for memory also has as its object only that which has been previously experienced. And in the case of a momentary object, there can be no such experience of what was previously experienced.

"It is logically consistent; for indeed, there is nothing that is not logically consistent when it is observed. [Objection: But how then did the author of the Bhāṣya say, "Where do we have the conviction that something is 'logically inconsistent'?
Listen:

As it has been said: "What is the impossibility of experience? For that which is experienced as experience itself—what need does it have for another experience? Therefore, it is well said: 'Where is there for us anything that is impossible'?"
“...conviction. Therefore, it is concluded that the aggregates (skandhas) are empty.
And likewise, the Brāhmaṇa also restates this very same meaning: “Having arisen from these elements as a mere mass of consciousness...”
"Along with them, one perishes; after death, there is no consciousness.
Therefore, these causes for the notion of a self in what is not-self have been presented by the venerable commentator as things to be rejected.
To this it is replied: this is not so; for when one has seen something on one day, on another day there arises the cognition, "I saw this."
There arises a recognition; and this occurs with respect to the inner self (pratyagātman), not with respect to another.
For that which saw [the object] on a previous day is "another" (para). Therefore, there exists another distinct from that [body], upon whom this word "I" depends.

But what is the reason for the rejection of inference here? We say it is because [inference] is impossible. To claim that "inference is not possible regarding an object perceived through direct perception" is sheer audacity; and he himself will state this later.
“Surely he perceives the eternal in the impermanent.
Therefore, it is not possible to explain this as having the intention of [pointing out] impossibility. Now, if it occurs to the mind that “the inference stated by the opponent is impossible,”
[Page 226] Thus it is said.

If it is asked, "For what purpose, then, is direct perception (pratyakṣa) presented? For inference is not possible when direct perception does not exist," then what is this phrase "when direct perception does not exist"?
Is this so? There is indeed inference that is independent of the operation of perception. We do not say that "inference never exists anywhere as being independent of the operation of perception."
What then? [The meaning is: "This inference does not proceed without one having first perceived the self for oneself through direct perception.
If it has been perceived by oneself, what is the use of inference? For [the purpose of inference] is the purification of one's own thorough knowledge.

[227] For the sake of the highest good; and this undertaking is for that purpose. Now, if this instruction is engaged solely for the benefit of others, what is the use of self-awareness at this point? Or, if it is for the sake of another's comprehension as well...
If perception alone is the valid means of knowledge, then the introduction of inference is useless.
Furthermore, as for what was said—"where this word 'I' [occurs]"—it is then again denied: "we do not..."
"We designate this word 'I', when it is employed in this sense, as the cause."

That too appears to be an assertion like that of one lacking intelligence: what is the purpose of introducing the word "I," which cannot be denied? This other point is also incorrect: "If there exists something other than consciousness...
“Let that cognizer and that cognition of his be demonstrated as ‘this is it’ and ‘it is such and such.’”

To the question [raised], the reply beginning with "In this regard, it is said" is not tenable; for here it was objected that if consciousness is not apprehended, there can be no apprehension of that [object]. How, then, can this objection be refuted by means of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedyatā*)?

For it is not the case that the apprehension of an object is preceded by the apprehension of consciousness, based on the fact that [consciousness] is self-cognized. Now, if the intention is this—that self-cognition cannot be designated as something distinct for another—this is stating too little; for how could it be cognized by another if it were not distinct?

Can this meaning be explained to another? Therefore, this too appears as if it were not preceded by due reflection. Furthermore, it is not at all understood what the purpose is in restating what has already been answered.

Nor has this point been abandoned, because of the concluding reference to the mention of "consciousness" (*vijñāna*). Now, if the intention is that even on the view that consciousness is mentioned, the perceptibility of the self cannot be denied, [then it is replied:
"We do not perceive any other form [of the self]."
Thus, this reasoning remains unrefuted; nor has any distinction been stated. Furthermore, by asserting the definition of analogy (upamāna) as propounded by the Naiyāyikas, [the author] himself—[p.

What has been stated contradicts the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇabhanga*). Furthermore, no clear answer is found even for the objection, "I am going. Moreover, this [position] that "I... is contrary to the knowledge of Brahman.

This notion of "I," which consists of the cognition of the object through its conditions, is proclaimed as the "anointed head" of the false knowledge of self in what is not-self—namely, egoism (*ahaṃkṛti*) and the sense of "mine" (*mama-kāra*). Those who know the Self consider the knowledge of the Self to be that which is free from egoism and the sense of "mine. Therefore, this [notion]—"I-cognition"—is merely a manifestation of the ignorance of the non-Self.

"The self is the object of knowledge"—to this it is replied: "On another day, regarding what was seen on a previous day, there arises the cognition, 'I saw this'; and this occurs with respect to the inner self (pratyagātman), not with respect to anything else."
What is this [thought],
"I saw this"? If it is indeed recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), then that is itself the refutation of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*).

It is not [the refutation] of selflessness (*nairātmya*). Nor is the negation of momentariness intended here. What then? It is the establishment of the existence of a self distinct from the intellect, the sense organs, and the body. Furthermore, selflessness was not asserted by others on the basis of momentariness; what then? On the basis of the non-perception of anything distinct from the aggregates (*skandha*), and [on the basis of their] permanence.

For it is momentariness that is contradictory, not the existence of a self; and here, the existence of that [self], which has been challenged by others, is being established, rather than a challenge to the permanence of a self that already exists. [p.

Concentration (*samādhi*). Nor does the mere fact that one perceiver was yesterday and another today constitute selflessness (*nairātmya*). Therefore, one should simply state: "There exists [a self] graspable by the notion of 'I', distinct from the body and the instruments [of perception]," rather than [specifying] "yesterday" or "today."
This [objection] is set aside. Now, if this thought arises:
"Even though existence has been established, because of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), the very nature of the self (*ātmatā*) is lost"—how then can there be liberation?
Why does the state of being aggregates (*skandhatā*) not likewise perish for the aggregates? For the nature of the self is indeed that of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*).

And the state of being an object of enjoyment belongs to the aggregates (*skandha*); and just as the state of being an object of enjoyment cannot be removed from the aggregates even if they are momentary, so too the state of being an enjoyer cannot be removed from the self (*ātman*). This, then, is like setting out on a journey at night.

You are ignorant of the self, you for whom such objections exist. Do you ask why the momentariness of the aggregates was taught? Or why it was taught? Because there is no experiencer. If there is no experiencer, [you ask] why the momentariness of the aggregates—does this constitute a royal edict? It is not a royal edict; it is a logical principle (*nyāya*).

This is indeed so. How? There is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for us that the instrument of action is momentary while the enjoyer exists. Why? Because the cause is to be inferred from the effect; and from that, the accomplishment of the action follows.

This doctrine of momentariness is based on the denial of action; and with the disappearance of action, there follows the denial of agency and enjoyership; and with that denial, there follows the denial of the self. This [world] is merely a nature of transformation.

"Effect and cause," and "agent and enjoyer"—this is merely a conceptual construction. Therefore, even though it is established that there is something distinct from the intellect, the senses, and the body as the mere substratum of the notion of "I," agency and enjoyment do not exist [inherently]; and the very nature of the self consists in being that [substratum]. Consequently, [the self] is preceded by indestructibility alone.
Thinking that there is a state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtā*), the author of the *Bhāṣya* has presented perception accompanied by recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).

For this very reason, the proponents of selflessness (*nairātmyavādin*) repeatedly attribute momentariness and inefficacy to the self, saying: "If it were like a hide, it would be impermanent; if it were like space, it would be equivalent to a non-entity."

Thus, it follows that the self is indeed the enjoyer. This is logical—that the self is the enjoyer; however, the attribution of agency is contradictory, because the self is actionless (*niṣkriya*), and its actionlessness follows from its omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*). This is well-established.

And there is omnipresence, because happiness is perceived everywhere. For nothing is contradicted if there is no coming. The state of being actionless was stated with reference to an action consisting of motion, but not with reference to experience.
Even in the case of its arising [from causes], it is therefore rightly said: "The self is precisely the agent and the enjoyer.
Consequently, this passage—"I saw this"—is logically established.
This is the recognition of the object.
"This is the basis for that"— this is presented in the section concerning words (*śabdādhikaraṇa*): "And this occurs with respect to the inner self (*pratyagātman*)."

For the sake of what purpose [is this said]? Precisely for the sake of establishing the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*). How so? Because enjoyment is observed in the inner self (*pratyagātman*). If the Supreme Self (*para*) were also to become an object of the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*), then it would follow that its status as an enjoyer is lost; yet it has been stated that the nature of being an enjoyer belongs to the Self. "Not in another, nor is the other... [and so forth].

[Otherwise], there would be no possibility of recognition [in the form]: "This is that very person who was seen on another day. If that is so, then for what purpose is the introduction of the word "I" in the phrase "where this word 'I' [is used]"; is it for the sake of denying [the existence of the self]? It is not for the sake of denial.
It is for the sake of others' understanding. Why, then, is there a denial? It is to dispel the suspicion that [the self] is a direct cause.
One who considers it to be a direct cause has demonstrated that "the word 'I' also exists with respect to what is not the self."
“[The word] ‘I’ is also seen used figuratively in reference to others,” and so forth;
[it is said: “We do not [hold this view].”

Thus, it has been made clear that this is not presented as a direct reason (*sākṣāddhetutayā*). Rather, the employment of the word is for the purpose of demonstrating the meaning of the reason. But surely, in the expression “I am going,” there is no meaning of a reason?

This can be refuted by way of mere illustration; for here, even the notion of "I" is observed to be inconstant, because the Self is immovable in nature. Therefore, one might suspect that the aggregates alone become the objective support; why then should this be regarded as beyond all doubt?
Is this understood? What is there to be doubted here? For the body and its instruments are grasped by this very cognition;
and with respect to an object grasped by one cognition, it is not possible for it to be the objective support of another contradictory cognition, as in the case of "the Vāhīka is a cow."
If it is argued that this is possible in a figurative sense (*gauṇa*),
you yourself have already refuted that. Therefore, the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) is indeed the undifferentiated cognition of "this" (*idampratyaya*) with respect to the self (*ātman*).

The object [of the teaching]. The Brāhmaṇa also restates this very same point: "He is indestructible, for he is not destroyed"—thus, by way of his indestructibility, the Self is the enjoyer; and "consciousness is perishable."

It brings about the state of having an object distinct from that [self]. Therefore, it cannot be said that this knot of the ego (ahaṃkāra) is a delusion, for "only that cognition whose instrument is defective and which possesses the conviction 'this is false' is an incorrect cognition; no other."
Since this matter is thus established:

if, at most, this is the conviction of those who know Brahman—that whatever is perceived is unreal, and that which is not perceived is the Reality—then salutations to them; and as for the rule that "no answer should be given to a learned man," this is the rebuttal in this case.
Therefore, this explanatory passage (arthavāda)— "This very sacrificer is equipped with the sacrificial implements"— is to be understood according to its literal meaning.
He said: "If there exists a knower other than consciousness, distinct from consciousness, let it be pointed out as 'this is it' and 'it is such-and-such'."
Why is this objection raised? This very thing is being objected to. That itself is not understood. How is it not understood? It is not understood in this way:
Is the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) regarding the self (*ātman*) accompanied by consciousness (*savijñāna*) presented as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such that this is said—?

Is it intended that consciousness (vijñāna), having set aside [its objects], should be demonstrated? For where knowledge has multiple things as its objective support, it is appropriate to say: "Set this aside and demonstrate that.
But here, consciousness is of a single, unitary nature. Therefore, the statement "this is to be excluded" is a mere word in the darkness.

To this it is replied: this is his intention; for if the self were an object of knowledge, it would be impossible to speak of cognition and the knower as distinct from it; nor is it established that consciousness exists apart from those two. [p.
Therefore, having set aside both the cognition and the cognizer as separate objects of knowledge, let it be demonstrated [as such].
To this it is replied: "It is self-cognizable; it cannot be seen by another."
What is the justification for this [conclusion]? Why is it not justified? It is not justified in this way:
namely, that this very same previously mentioned state of a single cognition having multiple aspects while having a single object would be admitted.
This is merely the fault of non-discrimination; there is no fault here on the part of your venerable self. But surely, this is the notion of "I"?
It is presented as "I saw this," not merely "I saw."
Thus it is said. And this being so, what is this "manifoldness of forms"? "Lack of discernment is the abode of supreme calamities.
For if the self—
If it were presented as being knowable by virtue of being expressible by words, or as being devoid of any other object of knowledge, then this objection would have arisen;
but here, consciousness is presented precisely as the cognizer of all that is knowable. Therefore, with respect to this—

How can this very presentation of a position be sublated by that same [position]? For it is not the case that what is sublated by something can itself be the sublater of that thing. Therefore, this is a correct response: "Just as someone with sight..."

By this illustration as well, the negation of any other agent or instrument is indeed firmly established. Now, one might object: "In this case, there is another agent and another instrument distinct from the object of cognition; so what is the point of this illustration? It is because of the commonality of the absence of any other agent. Therefore, [the means of knowledge] are free from defects in their causes and are non-erroneous.

And consciousness (*saṃvit*) is the proof for the existence of the self (*ātman*). Whether there be another agent or not, it has been said: "In whatever way objects are cognized, in that same way they exist; as they are not..."
"Objects are perceived, yet they do not exist [in that way]. On this point also, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage:
"When speech has become silent.
When the self is occupied elsewhere as an agent, how can it be an agent?

The question is: "Is the absence of other instruments perceived? And the mention of speech is for the purpose of illustrating the absence of other instruments. The meaning of the statement, "O Emperor, the light is the Self," is as follows.
It has been demonstrated by way of the refutation of the prima facie and final positions; and thus [it is said]: "The ungraspable is not grasped.
This is consistent with the Brāhmaṇa. But has it not been argued here that [the Self] is indeed ungraspable?
Have you not heard, "O Emperor, the Self is light"? Have you not heard this as well?

What is the reasoning for the claim that, in accordance with two other scriptural passages, this scriptural statement regarding its non-apprehensibility is merely relative, whereas the statement regarding the apprehension of the Self is not explained otherwise? For, in the case of the apprehension of the Self as self-luminous, figurative description (guṇavāda) is impossible;
moreover, non-apprehensibility is logically established as being relative, as in the injunction: "The Self is to be known, it is to be reflected upon."
And because there is no contradiction in this way, self-luminosity is thus established.
But if this is so, how can it be communicated to another? [p. 246] To produce conviction in another—

And this is the purpose of the undertaking of the authors of the treatises and the scriptures: that self-awareness itself (*svasaṃvid*) is established here as the means—namely, that one is aware by oneself and not by another.
