Since there exists in all persons an awareness that is not cognizable by another, the status of the teachings as "teachings" is established by way of negating the awareness of another.
This is what has been presented as "not this, not this.
Now, one might object: pleasure and the like are also indeed self-cognized;
they too are not cognized by another as residing in another. How, then, can [the Self] be distinct from them?
Is the Self taught? In that regard, the Commentator states: "They are indeed understood by another through being cognizable by means of indicative marks."
This has been said; but that is incorrect, because it would follow [absurdly] that the self (*ātman*) [is also non-existent].

In that regard, he himself sets forth the inference from purposeful action (*ceṣṭā*). Therefore, how can that which subverts an established fact be written by the learned? This objection belongs to one who has not served a teacher; for purposeful action [arises] from a defect in its cause—

[The former] is presented as being established through exclusion (*nirākaraṇatayā*); pleasure and the like, however, are understood through the knitting of eyebrows, the play of the eyes, and so forth. What, then, is the distinction between these two? By this [latter] as well, it is the cognition of another that is apprehended. Thus, it is not [produced] as an effect (*akāryata*).

[This is] the distinction. But how does one perceive that which is unconnected? Or how does a person, when not perceiving [error], dispel the suspicion of error regarding himself by means of the absence of error in others? We reply: "By the non-perception of error. And it has already been stated that in the case of non-perception, the state of being related is of no use. Therefore, this is logically consistent.

This is the statement of Śabara: "Let it be that there is no inference of one's own self; however, why does the cognition of another's self—which is caused by their activity—not lead to an inference of that other self? To this we reply: it has already been stated [on p. 249].
“For the selfhood [of the self] consists in being the enjoyer.

Here too, the analogy is presented merely as a means for explaining. And since that explanation is preceded by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no contradiction between the definition and its practical application. As for what is further said:
“Setting aside consciousness, let that [object] be demonstrated. But has this not already been answered by the statement: “It is self-cognized”?

"He becomes [that]"; furthermore, it is not logical to restate what has already been answered. Now, if this is the intended meaning—that this is not at all the answer to that—then to what, then, does that answer apply? If not...

Regarding the response to someone: must it necessarily be a response to that [previous question] merely by virtue of its occurrence? Surely it is understood to be a response to that because it is stated immediately after it; yet, know that it is not a response because another question is subsequently stated.
And by sequence, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is stronger. This [objection] is like wandering in the sky; both [points] are its very answer.
Even this statement, "He becomes self-cognizable," is understood to be an answer based precisely on the indicative mark; thus it has been explained.

And he possesses the capacity to remove that [ignorance]. Now, for what purpose is this further question? There is something still clinging [to him]. What is that which clings? Truly, it is the thought: "I know this."

It is experienced as such, and there is no postulation of another form; however, the apprehension of that which is distinct from consciousness is not possible, because activity is understood [to belong to it]; and when consciousness is understood, no other form is perceived.

Furthermore, it is emptiness. Therefore, this knot of ego-grasping (*ahaṅkāra*) is merely imagined; this is what is restated. What is the intended meaning of the respondent when he says, "If you negate the means itself"?
This is what is intended: for it has been stated that the apprehension conforms to the apprehended (*grāhya*), not that it conforms to the apprehender (*grāhaka*).
Since the state of being engaged [in activity] was presented as the means (*upāya*), how can the goal (*upeya*) be explained if the means is not employed?
Thus he says: “If you deny the very means, it is impossible to attain the goal without the means.”
“This indeed is the means for knowing objects that are to be known. “For example: what is called ‘white’? That in which whiteness exists.”
What is established by this?
This is established: that an object of cognition is not apprehended apart from its whiteness.

But surely, in this way, the cognition of the object to be known would be preceded by whiteness; and thus, an unintended consequence would be established. It is not an unintended consequence; for all that has been stated by this is: "there is no status as an end (*upeya*) for ends without a means (*upāya*). In whatever manner something possesses the status of a means, it is so for that [end]; such is the case with knowledge.

It has been stated that even though [the senses] serve as instruments, consciousness does not have them as its precursor. Therefore, for the Self, which is the object of all cognitions, there remains the state: "I perceived this.
To this extent...

The distinction is as follows: even in inference and other means of knowledge, there is direct perception (*pratyakṣatā*). For the difference in the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) arises from a difference in the object (*viṣaya*), not from a difference in the cognizer (*pramātṛ*). Furthermore, it is not even to be suspected that cognition possesses the nature of a cognizer; indeed, such a suspicion is impossible.

Because that is the reality. And this is rightly not to be doubted, since action—which possesses an object—is directed toward its object. As for the claim that the very nature of the knower cannot be understood apart from knowledge, that is because the understanding of it is dependent upon that [knowledge]; as it has been said: "And there is no perception of another form."
Thus,
that too has been refuted: "Granted, consciousness might be denied, but not the object."
Thus, it is established that the reality of the self exists.
As for the Brāhmaṇa passage, "After death, there is no consciousness," [it refers to a specific state].

Thus, that has been explained by the Brāhmaṇa itself through its preceding and succeeding arguments; and in this way, its status as an explanatory passage (arthavāda) is indeed established, as it is said:
"And this is not an injunctive word."
This too has been answered. But surely, the phrase "this very one" (sa eṣaḥ) is logically consistent;
“How is it that ‘one goes to the heavenly world’? It is established because the desires of the qualified person are fulfilled. As it has been said:
‘The notions of “I-making” and “mine-making” are the conceits of self in what is not-self.’”

Thus, this is to be spoken only to those whose impurities have been rubbed away, and not to those attached to action; hence it is concluded. And the Blessed Lord Dvaipāyana has said: "One should not create a disturbance of the intellect in the ignorant who are attached to action."
Thus, in the section on the secret [teachings],
it was not explained here by the venerable commentator because of conformity with the scriptural statement,
and not out of ignorance.
Some maintain that there is action in that state, because it is observed there.
“It has been stated that the relationship between word and meaning is eternal; that is untenable.
What is this untenability? This very thing is the untenability: [if] the word is non-eternal, [how can the relationship be] eternal?

"The relationship between word and meaning is not tenable. How then is it [tenable] in the case of inherence (*samavāya*)? Because it is untenable for two things that are established separately (*yutasiddha*). Furthermore, "word-ness" (*śabdatva*) has been refuted. But surely there exists something else, such as "the nature of *g*-ness" (*gatva*), which has not been refuted?
That is not so, because no distinction in the sound itself is perceived. How then is it [distinguished] among parrots, starlings, and humans?
Precisely for that reason, no intrinsic distinction is perceived; rather, it is the parrots, starlings, and humans themselves [who differ].
For in that case, they attain a state of distinction; and thus worldly people say, "This parrot recites," or "This man recites."
Thus they express the particulars in a general way, and not by saying, "this specific cow," or "that specific cow.
Therefore, the eternality of the relationship is not established.
Therefore, the eternity of the word must be asserted; this is stated, preceded by an objection, as: "Some [hold that the relationship is] produced, because it is observed therein.
But if this were so, even a produced relationship would not be tenable.

What follows from that? The cessation of worldly conventions. What follows from that in turn? The proposition of impermanence becomes untenable; because it contradicts worldly conventions, permanence would necessarily follow by force of logic.

"Let there be no impermanence [of the word], because it would contradict worldly convention; what follows from the consequence that it must be permanent? This follows: namely, the very impossibility of worldly convention. "True, this is so, provided that [the word] has been completely set aside by convention; for there is nothing that is not an object of convention. This [convention] is the remover of the distress caused by all such logical impossibilities.

[Page 261] This is the established convention (*samaya*). Therefore, for those who hold verbal testimony to be a valid means of knowledge (*śabdapramāṇaka*), validity is not established merely by observing worldly usage. Consequently, an effort must be made toward the eternity of the expression; and this—

[The opponent] objects: [The Veda] must have had a beginning, because the knowledge of the relationship [between word and meaning] is preceded by the linguistic usage of elders, and the comprehension of meaning is preceded by the knowledge of that relationship. Nor can its status as a valid means of knowledge be established on the grounds of momentariness alone, as in the case of the eye and other senses, because there is no comprehension upon the first hearing. [The Siddhāntin replies: "Some say it is [authoritative] action, because it is seen therein."
Thus, the producedness (*kṛtakatva*) of sound is stated; what is this producedness? It is arising through human effort. But is it not [the case that] without effort—

[Objection: Even the prior production of sound is observed, as in the case of *chala* (equivocation), *utthāpanā* (refutation), and so forth. [Reply: This is not a fault, because the present discussion concerns verbal expression (*abhidhāna*). Furthermore, this verbal expression is never seen to be uncaused by effort. Therefore, since it is perceived immediately following an action, we conclude that it is produced by that very action. [Objection: How then is it in the case of roots, water, and the like?

Because its existence is understood from other sources; whereas in the case of sound, perception occurs only immediately after effort. Therefore, it cannot be said that effort is a manifestor of something already existing.
[Objection: But is there not this proof for its existence prior to effort? [Reply: What is this? It is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).

[Page 263] It is perception. How, then, is there recognition here, given that no difference is perceived? Or does one who maintains the doctrine of impermanence perceive any difference at all? Why is there none between what has been destroyed and what has arisen? Because of the absence of distinguishing features—
Because of apprehension. Is recognition based solely on the non-apprehension of specific differences?
Or what do you think? Recognition would then also apply to action. This is said when there is apprehension of the essential nature;
and it has been stated that action is inferential. What, then, is the status regarding flames and the like? [If they were] eternal...

If it is argued that there is a contradiction with inference regarding flames and the like, that is equally applicable even when [the sound] is uttered, because of its non-abiding nature and so forth.

Therefore, even when no specific difference is perceived, there is distinctness; and since this distinctness is established, [sound is impermanent] due to its being perceived immediately after an effort.

[Sound] arises from effort. [Objection: But even for those things produced by effort, there is no impossibility of linguistic usage because they persist for a period of time; the innate capacity of the eye and other organs to perceive form is not at all obstructed even after they have been produced. [Reply: True; but this is not the case with sound, because it does not endure. [Objection: But is it not the case that the eye does not endure? *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical structure of the argument regarding the non-permanence of sound versus the persistence of sense organs.*

If it is argued that even when the ear is damaged, the capacity to perceive form is not at all impaired, and the same should hold for sound, this has already been refuted by the fact that there is no comprehension upon the first hearing. Therefore, [the argument fails] because of "impossibility" (asthānāt).

Thus, this reason [of momentariness] destroys the innate nature of the relationship [between word and meaning]. If there were persistence over a period of time, then comprehension of the meaning from the word through linguistic usage might indeed occur; however, if there is no persistence, then convention alone is the refuge.
It has been stated that it ought to be so: “because of the impossibility.”
Even worldly usage follows this very same principle. What here is the following of that principle?
It is the primary sense of the verb *karoti* (to do/make): "Make a sound," "Do not make a sound," "This person is making a sound."
"O young brahmin! [he said].
“And we perceive sound simultaneously in various locations; therefore, it is untenable for it to be a single, eternal entity.
What is this untenability? This is the untenability: that the simultaneous perception of a single thing in multiple places is not possible.

It has been seen. What follows from that? This results from it: difference has been established. But surely, difference has already been established. True, it has been established; however, the accumulation of reasons is now being demonstrated.

What is the gain? Indeed, none at all. If there is no gain, what is the use of this accumulation of reasons? True, as you have said; however, this very point challenges our established conclusion (*rāddhānta*). Therefore, this undertaking is for the purpose of refuting that delusion; for it is not possible to declare something to be erroneous unless it has first been presented.
And if its erroneous nature were not demonstrated, this [work] would be redundant for someone of dull intellect;
furthermore, this treatise is intended for all purposes, as was shown by the author of the Commentary with the words, "even by one whose poison is mild."
“If there is no distinction, there is no plurality for that which is eternal”— what does this mean? Does it mean that “if there is no distinction, there is no manifoldness”?

Thus it can be said whether [the object] is eternal or non-eternal; we do not know what is meant by the mention of "eternal. If multiplicity were to exist even for a non-eternal thing despite the absence of any distinction, then it would be logical [to speak of it].
In order to say "of the eternal," this passage must therefore be explained. It is now explained as follows:
The simultaneous perception of a single entity, such as a cow, in multiple locations is observed in the case of that which is eternal; therefore, by this [argument],
the objection that "because of simultaneity in other beings" is rendered otherwise established (anyathāsiddhi) is raised.
The answer to this is: "In the absence of a distinction.
Is there a distinction in the case of a cow and so forth? For that too is one and undifferentiated; for it is not one thing in a brindled cow and another in a black cow.

Now, if this is the intention—that [simultaneous perception occurs] even when there is no specific difference in the substratum—then in that case too, it is only the substratum that is different; what has been gained for the thing residing in that substratum? Therefore, the simultaneous perception of a single eternal entity in multiple locations is observed.
Consequently, simultaneous perception is not a valid reason for [establishing] difference. Now, suppose this view is held:

[269] There is no simultaneous perception of a cow or the like in multiple locations; for in that case, it is only the individual differences (*bheda*) themselves that are apprehended as being in various places, not the universal "cowness" (*gotva*). How then is there the cognition "cow" with respect to all of them?
Is there not the cognition "cow"?
For this very reason, cowness does not have multiple locations; otherwise, one would indeed perceive "cowness is here."
In that case, one would have to say, "here is cowness. How then is it said, "inherence [is known] from this cognition"?

That statement intends the category of a single substance (*ekadravyapadārtha*), not individual instances (*vyakti*). Therefore, simultaneous perception serves as the reason for their difference, provided that no specific distinction exists.
Thus, the mention of a "distinction" (viśeṣa) is appropriate. [Objection:
But even for that which is impermanent, there can be no difference in the absence of a distinction. [Reply: Certainly, such a distinction exists in the case of flames and the like;
moreover, because it is an effect, there is no contradiction. However, since that which is eternal is not an effect, its multiplicity would be contradictory; therefore, the reason [adduced] is valid.

[Page 271] Furthermore, those who know the science of words (śabdajña) maintain that there is a relationship of original nature and its modification (prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva); and this is not possible for that which is eternal.
Therefore, even traditional authority (smṛti) is indeed consistent with the previously stated reasons. We also perceive that similarity (sādṛśya) is likewise consistent.
Thus, its status as an effect is established.
And because it follows the increase of its cause, we consider it to be an effect, just like a flame and so forth.
Therefore, even though its parts are not perceived, an increase in its parts is inferred; in this case, it is indeed a flame.
An illustration.
"But the vision there is equal. What is this "equal vision"? This is that equal [vision].
"Darśana"—the reason is the same whether it concerns what is to be done or what is not to be done. How is there equality?
By virtue of being a renouncer (*sāṃnyāsikatayā*). What has been renounced here? This has been renounced here:
namely, that we shall state [the object] as being graspable by perception accompanied by recognition (*sapratyabhijña*). But was this not already stated and refuted?

And—just as in the case of flames and the like, it is not possible to assert identity when there is a counter-argument based on inference—this is true; provided that recognition were said to be based solely on the non-apprehension of difference. We shall demonstrate, however, that it is based on the apprehension of that [identity]. Therefore, the statement "But the perception there is the same" is well-founded.
Thus [it is said].
“The non-perception of an existing thing is due to the non-arrival of the object”—
this argument of theirs is likewise inconclusive.
It has been stated that "even perception [is impossible]. But this is not tenable; what is the cause for the non-perception of that which is eternal?

If you say it is simply the non-arrival of the object, then let it be so. However, that very point is difficult to maintain here. Why? Because, on the theory of eternality, sound is something to be manifested (*abhivyaṅgya*); and this sound is one and has a single locus, since its locus is space (*ākāśa*).

And its apprehender is space alone; what then is this "non-arrival at the object"? Therefore, it is logical that there is non-perception precisely of that which has been destroyed. By whom was it said that this is not logical? But when there is the apprehension of that [destruction], it is logical that everything else is illogical. For this very reason it was said: "If we are able."
Thus it is said.
275] But even if that [object] is apprehended, does not the postulation of an obscuration and so forth find no footing here? Why is that?
Because it contradicts what was previously established. What was established? That space (*ākāśa*) is the sense organ (*indriya*), and that is one.

Therefore, even though conjunctions and disjunctions act as manifestors, it would follow that all sounds are perceived by all [sense organs]. While it might be reasonable for there to be perception by all [organs], it is not [the case] for all sounds.
This is logical, because the manifestors [of a permanent entity] are distinct from its causes. Furthermore, perception by all [perceivers] is exactly the same even in the case of an effect.

As for the objection that a fault shared by both sides cannot be leveled against one alone—this refutation has already been addressed by stating the distinction between a producer (*kāraka*) and a manifestor (*abhivyañjaka*); otherwise, those who maintain the doctrine of permanence would not have been subject to such an objection.
[276] There is this distinction: would the manifestation (*abhivyakti*) belong to the sound or to the sense organ?
Regarding the manifestation of the sound first, since all sounds have a single object—just as in the case of jars and other objects—[they would all be manifested simultaneously].

It cannot be said that the manifestation of objects occurs sequentially, because such a sequence is not observed in well-known manifestors such as lamps; however, in the case of causes, an inference regarding their capacity is possible because the effect is observed. [Objection: But surely, even in the case of manifestors, an inference is possible precisely because their manifestation is observed.
It is logical on account of capacity; it is not possible as a counter-argument to the position that [the effect] pre-exists. What, then, is the distinction?
Because [causal efficiency] is observed in well-known causes and is not observed in mere manifestors, it conforms to what is seen.

And this is not contradicted by perception; nor is it contradicted by inference. But surely, if they have the same object, there is a contradiction; whereas if they have different objects, the talk of contradiction is itself contradictory. True; however, the very fact that they have different objects is difficult to state here. It is not difficult to state. For it is accepted that the ear is space (*ākāśa*), and space is non-different [from one another]; and all sounds are [perceived by] the ear—

[The opponent says: "There are objects; therefore, there is identity of object; and from the identity of the object, there is contradiction with perception. [The author asks: What is this that you are prattling?
This is truly fallen into the category of the proverb: "Touched on the ear, he wiggles his hips."

The object of manifestation is being defined, not that of the word itself; moreover, this object is distinct from the objects of a lamp or similar things. Therefore, it has been stated that because there is no contradiction with lamps and the like, one cannot claim a contradiction with the inference regarding the manifestor in the case of the word. Consequently, the inference based on its apprehension is difficult to refute.

Therefore, this non-perception [of the sound] is now stated to be inconclusive. But surely, manifestation has the auditory organ as its object, not the sound as its object; for it is only when the auditory organ is manifested that it perceives the sound—this much is the case regarding the manifestor.
It is an inference based on capacity (*śakti*), for there is no contact with the notion that "this word is this" or "it is not that.
[This refers to] the manifestors. And this indeed is the established conclusion (siddhānta). It has been stated that this very [conclusion] is contradicted by inference.
True; it is improper to subvert well-known inference. It is likewise improper to subvert well-known perception.

Perception, which possesses recognition, is established with respect to the self and to universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth. Since both [perception and inference] are uncontradicted, and because no object whatsoever would be established [otherwise], one of them must be sublated; for the Naiyāyikas hold that perception is stronger than inference. But is it not the case that perception can be subject to error? And in inference as well, there is delusion—

The learned reply: We do not say that there is no error even in inference; rather, we maintain that because of the non-apprehension of difference (*bhedāgrahaṇa*), the cognition of "that" arises even with respect to what is "not-that. We consider perception itself to be weak when it is subject to possible error. It is for this very reason—that it reveals the causes of both manifest and unmanifest error—that the experts in logic have stated: "Indeed, perception..."
"Furthermore, inference is stronger.

Is it the fact that the cause is known to be defective that is being put forward here? What follows if it is so put forward? But surely, because of the absence of its opposite, it cannot be put forward as existing at all.

It is possible. Is inversion alone the cause of falsity? A defect in the cause has also been presented as being due to its being an improper cause. But was it not stated that a defect in the cause is something to be perceived through effort? What is this?
What is this that is called "effort" (prayatna), which is said here not to exist? This very thing is effort:

having recognized a defect in the cause elsewhere through its contrary nature, one understands—precisely because it occurs when that [defect] is present—that "this error is caused by this"; and once that is known, even though the error is no longer present, one recognizes [the previous state as] "delusion."
One determines, "This is silver. What exists here that is of such a nature? Certainly, there is the non-apprehension of difference (*bhedāgrahaṇa*);

it is precisely based on the non-apprehension of difference that the delusion of silver occurs in relation to mother-of-pearl and similar objects. So too, in this case, there is the non-apprehension of difference.
The delusion regarding that [word-form] in respect to the object is based solely on a connection, just as in the case of a flame and so forth. Therefore, it has been well said:
"The apprehension of that [word-form] in the word itself is an error. This applies to one for whom the form of the object is indeed contrary [to its true nature].

Knowledge arises only occasionally; for that [knowledge], it is appropriate to say, "Because there is no error, this is not a delusion. But for one for whom error is based solely on non-apprehension, however—

What power is there to assert a difference from flames and the like when there is a contradiction with inference? But surely, non-apprehension is also determined by subsequent apprehension. And here, in no state whatsoever is there an apprehension of difference, as in the case of the *saugandhika* flower and crystal. How then is it in the case of flames and the like?

If it is argued that the comprehension [of the object] arises from inference, that is equally applicable here as well. Therefore, the claim of the Mīmāṃsakas that perception, accompanied by recognition, has sound as its object is merely a snare of hope. As for what has been stated by others— [p. 283]

It may be argued that even when the object to be refined is the same, a difference in the effect is observed due to a difference in the refinement—just as those whose eyes have been smeared with the fat of a frog see bamboo stalks as if they were snakes. But this is merely a display of empty talk; for that which is called "refinement" (saṃskāra) is precisely that which generates a capacity for its own specific effect.

Furthermore, this apprehension of an object as it is not (ayathārtha-grahaṇa) is not the function of the sense organ; it has been established that this is based solely on non-apprehension (agrahaṇa). Therefore, even though there is no difference [in the nature] of the object to be refined (saṃskārya), since there is no difference in the effect due to the difference in the refinement (saṃskāra)—as there is none in the case of a cognizer—something else must be pointed out. And as for that which—
It is said that a face is manifested differently in a sword, a mirror, and so forth; what is meant by this?
It is observed that this coloring (uparāga) occurs in the object of perception (grāhya), and it is logical, because the manifestor (abhivyañjaka) also falls within the scope of the objective domain.

In this case, however, the auditory organ is not something that can be grasped, nor are conjunction and disjunction. Therefore, this too is merely a manifestation of space (ākāśa). Consequently, the claim that "sound is eternal" must be accepted solely on the basis of faith.
Since the Veda consists of sound, one must avoid censuring it; for the authors of the Dharmaśāstras have declared: "The atheist who reviles the Veda is to be cast out by the virtuous.
Therefore, [this is] not [the case].

In this matter, primacy alone is the refuge; it is not possible, however, to argue logically for independence on the grounds of the eternity of sound. Let us postulate some eminent sage, the Blessed One, who is free from passion and the like, possesses unimpeded knowledge, and has a mind permeated with compassion; or else, let us resort to the view of Bṛhaspati.

[Page 285] We observe that this which is declared in the three Vedas is merely conventional usage (*vyavahāra-mātra*), maintained by the wise as a well-established convention for the sake of accomplishing the worldly course of life. We consider this alone to be reasonable; for when something is perceived...

It is logical that the postulation of the unseen (adṛṣṭa) occurs only when it is possible; for this fact is observed—that the wise rely upon those who are straightforward. And just as even for those who maintain the authority of scripture (āgama), its lack of validity is established by the observation of a motive, as in:
"They practice the gift of elephants with their trunks [as sacrificial posts]."
In such cases as these,
one must either exert effort to establish that sound is the object of perception accompanied by recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), or else explain how it is so for flames and the like.

Or can their difference be understood through inference? But was it not just said, "through inference"? What is that inference? It is the disparity regarding non-manifestors. But has it not been observed that the capacity of manifestors extends to multiple objects? But this inference concerns the manifestor; how then can it concern something else?

Is inference the cause for the delimitation of an object other [than the one perceived]? For it is the manifesting refinement (*abhivyañjaka-saṃskāra*) that obstructs the ear, and not that which makes known the distinctness of the sound. But was it not said: "If conjunctions and disjunctions do not produce a refinement capable of enabling the ear to grasp the sound..."?
The producers of the sound would [themselves] be produced; and if there is production, there is difference.
How does the negation of one thing imply the production of another? Because otherwise, the operation [of the cause] would be inexplicable. It is not so.

If the *saṃskāras* (dispositions) were to effect a refinement (*saṃskāra*), what else could there be other than the production of sound? Must that which cannot logically function as a refiner necessarily be a producer? If it is not a producer, it would be entirely devoid of activity; moreover, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and disjunction (*vibhāga*) are observed to have other purposes. True.

Let them be producers or transformers of that for whose sake they exist; and since their purpose is established as being for the sake of another's comprehension, let whatever is desired regarding those two be postulated. However, in the case of a different object, since there is no connection, what basis would there be for such a postulation? Therefore, conjunction and disjunction must have causality toward something other [than themselves].

How do the Naiyāyikas think? They think as follows: "If there is no effect in the auditory organ, we perceive the effect in the sound. Is its being for that purpose (tādarthya) established through its being an effect?

It is said: "Om. Then the effect is established in the auditory organ; the experts in sound (śabdavidaḥ) maintain that conjunctions and disjunctions are not the objects of the word. But is it not improper for the experts in sound to say this on the basis of observing an effect? They reply: there is no observation of an effect whatsoever in the case of sound.
Because that [sound] is what is apprehended. What, then, do conjunctions and disjunctions perform? We say: they effect the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the auditory organ.
But was it not already argued that a distinction from other types of refinement is not logically established here?
You consider the absence of the effect to be established through inference; we, however, do not accept production on the basis of perception.

And it is an established principle that, between perception and inference, perception is more authoritative. But surely it was stated that non-apprehension is the cause of error, as in the case of [the perceived continuity of] a flame and so forth; yet here, non-apprehension itself is unestablished.
In that regard, how so? Through inference from an effect (*kāryānumāna*). But here, even now, that [effect] is not established;
and what is unestablished is not sufficient for proof. Furthermore, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is established because it is independent.

Or what need is there for inference? This is precisely the need: that once inference is established, the effect [of sound] is proven, and once the effect exists, inference is established; however, perception does not depend on the apprehension of that [sound] in such a manner, for its apprehension arises from perception alone. Furthermore, conjunction and disjunction are well-known from other sources as being objects of the sense of hearing.
From what else? It has been stated, "Because seeing is for the sake of another," according to worldly convention. Therefore:

When something serves a particular purpose, the function should be postulated in whatever way is possible. It has been stated that the intended meaning (tātparya) does not arise from the function itself, because it cannot be understood through any other means. Therefore, there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) here for [the existence of the cause], as there is in the case of a flame and so forth. Consequently, "there is no perception of the existent after [its destruction]."
Thus, the inconclusiveness [of the reason] is established.

How, then, can it be maintained that manifestation has only a single object? Since the existence of an unperceived entity is postulated on the basis of observing its effect, there can be no denial of that perceived grasping.
It is logical. However, because another effect is observed, it is indeed logical to postulate a difference in the cause.
292] "When conjunction and disjunction have ceased..."
Thus, what are those conjunctions and disjunctions intended?
We say they belong to the palate and other [articulatory organs]. Why is this so? Because of the hearing of the words "when they have ceased";
whereas the production and cessation of the aerial elements are to be inferred. [As it is said: "They do not indeed cease."
What is the intended meaning? Having in mind the conjunctions and disjunctions pertaining to air,
this reply— "for they are not perceptible"— is given because they are to be understood through their effects.
— Thus it has been made clear. If this is so, then the subsequent passage, beginning with "because its object is space," would not be tenable.
“Because space is one.

How is this not tenable? If the air-currents were the manifesters [of sound], then, as in the case of the view that sound is produced, it would necessarily follow that the sound is perceived only where those air-currents are present.

Thus, this is not tenable. Now, if the intention is as follows: in the theory of manifestation (*abhivyakti*), sounds do not reside in the air at all; rather, they reside only in space (*ākāśa*). For those, however, for whom [sounds] are produced...
The conjunctions and disjunctions belonging to air serve as the non-inherent causes (asamavāyikāraṇa) for them;

that very [air] becomes the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa). It is logical that the effect is perceived precisely where the cause exists. Thus, when this is understood, the manifestation of the conjunctions and disjunctions belonging to air [is established].

Regarding causality, wherever there is a manifestor, there alone is manifestation; just as wherever there is a cause, there alone is the effect. Now, if you think that this is appropriate for an effect but not for manifestation, that is incorrect; for manifestation itself is indeed an effect, whereas the manifested object—

[It is] previously arisen; therefore, since manifestation occurs in a particular location, perception occurs in that very same place—this is equal for both positions. Consequently, this passage must be explained. The "Beloved of the Gods" (the King) is ignorant of the distinction.
For an effect indeed occupies the location of its cause; however, that which is not an effect does not depend on another for its location.

Therefore, let manifestation occur in the location of the manifestor; but why should the manifested object itself occupy that location, given that it is not produced by it? [This is because] that location is what is intended to be the manifested object.

And because the locus of sound is space, which is unitary, it would follow that it is perceived by everyone, even when the conjunctions and disjunctions of air have been cognized, since space is one for all auditory organs. True; as follows:

You have said: "If conjunctions and disjunctions were the manifestors of sound, they would be the manifestors of the auditory organ (*śrotra*); and for the auditory organ, its location is indeed the locus of the hearer. But surely, the auditory organ is just space (*ākāśa*), and that is equally present elsewhere as well in the manifestation of sound. To this it is replied: True.

Space is one and the same everywhere; however, its state as the auditory organ exists only in the location of the hearer, because it functions as an instrument [only] through its connection with an agent.
Since agency resides only in the location of the body by virtue of being the locus of the agent's experience, there is no equality [between all locations].
Therefore, just as in the case of production, there is no perception by everyone even in the case of manifestation. "This is not so;"
"If they assist without having reached [the object], then those situated in near and distant places would perceive the sound simultaneously.
But, one might object, in the view that the auditory organ (*śrotra*) is refined [by the sound], "the auditory organ situated at a distance is not refined."

By saying this, it is stated that the refinement (*saṃskāra*) occurs only through contact (*prāpti*); and in the absence of contact, the very designation of "far" and "near" would not be possible. What is this [statement], "if they assist without being contacted"? There is no possibility of them being uncontacted, because [the text says] "being far away."
Because it is so stated [in the text].

Therefore, we do not know how this commentary came to be composed. It has come about as follows: according to the view that the auditory organ is refined (*saṃskāra*), since sound is omnipresent (*sarvagata*), to whatever extent the refinement is inferred by its effect, to that extent—

[Page 298] It would follow that there is simultaneous apprehension. What is the intended meaning? Is it not the case that the conjunctions and disjunctions consisting of air are not capable of refining the auditory organ without reaching it? For by means of conjunctions and disjunctions, no conjunction—
It cannot be said that another division is being commenced, because both [alternatives] would follow as a consequence;

for it is not logical to postulate two causes for a single effect, since an effect makes known its cause, but does not likewise make known another effect. Therefore, this is consistent only with the theory of production—that is, as long as there is momentum.

It is conjunctions and disjunctions that initiate an effect, and not so in the case of the theory of manifestation (*abhivyakti*). But surely, even in the theory of effect (*kāryapakṣa*), the postulation of another effect is not at all tenable? True, it is not tenable; [yet it is accepted].

The perception of another effect, however, is indeed perceptible, because it is perceived in succession by those situated far away and those situated nearby. But is this not the same even in the case of manifestation? It is not the same; for manifestation does not initiate another manifestation, whereas there is no contradiction whatsoever in an effect initiating another effect; for an effect can indeed be relative.

And it is the cause; it is not, however, that manifestation is the manifester. Therefore, those situated far away and those situated nearby perceive the sound simultaneously, to whatever extent it is perceived. Consequently, this objection is valid.

To say that illumination requires another illumination is the talk of a fool. Therefore, let the conjunctions and disjunctions of air initiate sound; or let the established doctrine of the followers of Ulūka (the Vaiśeṣikas) prevail:
"The production of sound results from conjunction, from disjunction, and from sound."
Thus [it is asked]: what is the purpose of demonstrating here that which has not been stated? What is this conceit, thinking "I too possess hearing regarding this"? This is not—

There may be the conceit of some ignorant person, thinking: "This conclusion was neither presented nor refuted by the venerable author of the Commentary (Bhāṣyakāra). To dispel that [notion], this is presented. By the very presentation of the word "air" (vāyu), this has been both presented and refuted, because the reasons for the presentation and the refutation are identical.
Therefore, this passage is intended to demonstrate the difference between the two positions—that of manifestation (*abhivyakti*) and that of an effect (*kārya*).
"This is not so; for the air-currents impelled by the impact [of the vocal organs] displace other stationary air-currents..."
"Being obstructed from all directions, they produce conjunctions and disjunctions and continue to proceed as long as their momentum lasts.
But is this not simply the same as what was called "producing"? And yet, "manifesting" was what was asserted.
[This concerns] conjunctions and disjunctions. Therefore, this appears entirely incoherent. Why so? Because you have said:
"It has been stated. You are ignorant of non-manifestation. What is this ignorance of non-manifestation?
This is the state of non-manifestation; for manifestation is indeed the removal of concealment. By whom was it said, "no"?
It has been stated that this very removal does not initiate another removal, for once the removal has occurred, there is no further effort required.

They are removers, yet they do not remove everything that is removable, just as the light of the sun and so forth [does not remove all darkness]. True; this fault would indeed arise if one were to postulate a single remover possessing multiple functions. However, in this case, there are many manifestors. How is this known? Or rather, in your own view regarding the theory of production (*kāryapakṣa*), there is a multiplicity of causes.

How so? If it is argued that it is because of the multiplicity of effects, then for me as well, there is a multiplicity of manifestors due to the multiplicity of manifestations. But how is there a multiplicity of manifestations? Just as there is a multiplicity of effects. [p. 305] Even if [the word-sound] were one...
Furthermore, we shall state again that it has been said that perception is more authoritative. And in the case of oneness, there is eternity;
and in the case of eternity, there is only a multiplicity of manifestations, not a multiplicity of effects—this is the established position.

Regarding the phrase "of the application": once this principle is established, the application [of the word] is accomplished just as in the case of cow-dung and the like, because a worldly sentence has as its object that which is already cognized by other means of valid knowledge.
[Page 306] “Just as this [appearance] belongs to a single existent,” [this statement] produces the delusion of multiplicity. But how so?

Can it be said that there is error in the absence of a misconception? [It cannot,] because a defect in the cause is perceived. Which cause is understood here to be defective? First, the object is certainly not defective, since it has not come within the range of the ear. Nor is the auditory organ defective, because it is clearly manifested. If, on the other hand, it is assumed that the auditory organ is "seen" [by inference], then in that case—

[Page 307] It follows that only the sound itself would be perceived, and there is nothing else to be grasped by the auditory organ apart from the sound. If this is so, then even in the view that [the universal] is an effect, how can there be an auditory perception of multiplicity? That is not indeed auditory; it is mental.
Indeed, that is so. Is it the case that an external object not grasped by the ear is grasped by the mind?
Or what is this "external object" intended by you that is distinct from sound—namely, this diversity of sounds (*śabdanānātva*)?
Is this diversity of sounds something distinct from sound, or is it sound itself? Or rather...

[Page 308] Is the property of sound something other than sound? First of all, this cannot be a property belonging to sound alone, because it is observed even in the case of visible forms and so forth; for visible forms and the like are also "various."

Thus it is understood. Nor is this [object] the sound itself, because we observe its distinction [from sound] in the statement, "the multiplicity of sound. Therefore, we do not know which sense organ [perceives it].

[If it is argued that] there must be an operation whose defectiveness could be postulated [as the cause of error], then is this plurality [of forms] simply ungraspable? Yet it is perceived in all objects. Furthermore, the view that [this plurality] consists of the form of cognition has been refuted by the Buddhists on the grounds of its being ungraspable. It is replied: if something is graspable, and when that [object] is grasped there is a reflective awareness (*avamarśa*) of another graspable [form], that is plurality. If that is so, then [let us consider] the ear itself.

[Page 309] There would be a defect in perception; and if there is a defect, the apprehension of the word does not occur. And if there is no apprehension of the word, how could there be a reflective awareness (*avamarśa*) of another word? Therefore, the defect must be attributed to the reflective awareness, and not to the apprehension of the word.

In that case, the fault lies with the mind (*manas*). But surely it cannot be said that even the mind is at fault, because when the auditory organ perceives, there is a perception of the object as it truly is; for it is not possible for one who has not grasped the correct object to have a reflective awareness (*avamarśa*) of that object.

Therefore, the gods will conceive this delusion because of non-inversion and because the faulty cause has not been ascertained. To designate something as a delusion when it is not a delusion is even more wicked than delusion itself. Therefore, those who know delusion must state the cause of delusion here. This is what is said: "It was stated by you yourself that [it cannot be perceived] without the external sense organ having been grasped..."
"It is grasped by the mind.

Since that [multiplicity] is grasped by the sense organ, it is established by perception that multiplicity does not exist; likewise, the apprehension of multiplicity by the mind is simply not possible.

What is its object, and what is the sense-faculty for the cognition of multiplicity? This is the sense-faculty and this is the object— since sounds located in various places arrive simultaneously, they are independent of one another.

In this way, they simultaneously initiate the refinements (*saṃskāra*) of the auditory organ; and due to the conformity of those refinements, one perceives even a single sound as if it were manifold. Because of the production of each refinement individually, the power [of the auditory organ]—like the visual power divided by fingers—perceives even a single [sound] as if it were distinct. Therefore, this [perception of multiplicity] is based on the non-apprehension of the distinction between the powers.
[Page 312] It is an error.

By this, the perception of an interval is refuted. But how, again, is the perception of an interval refuted by this? It is indeed reasonable that the awakening of a capacity occurs due to a difference in mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).
The power (*śakti*), which conforms to that [object], though single, presents even a single object as divided;
thus, due to the non-apprehension of its own internal differentiation, it produces the illusion of apprehending many things. What is the cause for the apprehension of the intervals?
Therefore, state another cause. It is not stated; this very thing is the cause. How so?

What is the reason? Sounds arising from various locations, initiating a refinement (*saṃskāra*) through their distinctness, produce an awakening of the power [of audition] up to its very root. Therefore, although the sound resides in the space of the auditory organ, it is perceived as if situated in that [external] location, due to the influence of the auxiliary factors (*anugrāhaka*). But surely, only the final conjunction and disjunction (*saṃyoga-vibhāga*) effects the refinement?

What is this sluggishness of yours? It is untenable that the final [conjunction] produces [the effect] without having been previously assisted by conjunction and disjunction; for the production of the effect occurs as if by the power of those assisting factors. And for this very reason—
The cessation of conditioned phenomena follows from their prior momentum; therefore, by producing effects in accordance with the arising of the self,
they cause that self to be understood in various ways.
“What is the purpose of this proposal: ‘Granted, the regions themselves may be distinct’?

[The sound] would reach [the ear] if the auditory faculty were to come to the location of the conjunctions and disjunctions; but this is not the case, as it has already been refuted in the Bhāṣya itself. For this very reason, it was said, "if one so desires" (*kāmam*). [Regarding] other beings—
The intention is that even in the case of a side (pakṣa), difference does not obtain. [Objection: But surely there is the perception of one thing in many places. [Reply:
This is the prattle of a fool; the objection regarding the perception of one thing in many places has already been refuted.
“Another sound is not a modification”;
for in this context, [the rule] “*iko yaṇ aci*” does not apply.

Thus, the relationship of original form (*prakṛti*) and modification (*vikāra*) is taught; for in common usage, those desiring to employ the sound *y* do not substitute the sound *i*. Furthermore, grammatical substitutions (*ādeśa*) apply to what is already established in common usage. Therefore, this meaning is prescriptive: when a vowel (*ac*) follows.

In place of the phoneme *i*, there is the phoneme *y*. However, similarity in the relationship between a base and its modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*) is not an absolute rule, as has been stated because such a relationship is not observed between a lump of curd and a lump of jasmine flowers; therefore, it is established that [the word with *y*] is a different word altogether.
“The increase of resonance (nādavṛddhi) is supreme,” which is equal [to the previous case] in its avoidance of distinction; for just as there,
distinct [sounds] cause one to understand what is distinct, so too here, accumulated [sounds] cause one to understand what is accumulated, while remaining in their divisions.
It is as if divided; therefore, an illusion arises as if it were large and as if it possessed parts.

It has been stated that the awakening of a capacity occurs in accordance with the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). Consequently, this too is due to the non-apprehension of the distinction between latent impressions.

The error lies precisely in the [logical] connection. Therefore, since perception accompanied by recognition is established, the previously stated collection of reasons for impermanence is rendered inconclusive.
[Page 319] Now, the status of sound as an object of perception accompanied by recognition is stated: “But it must be eternal,
because its manifestation is for the sake of another.”
Thus [it is said]: "Because perception is for the sake of another.

Of what is this the reason? It is the reason for the eternity of sound. But is this not a property that does not belong to the subject (*apakṣadharma*)? And since it is not a property of the subject...
The Naiyāyikas maintain that there is no causal efficacy [in the word]. For they have not heard the scriptures. Here, it is perception itself that is presented as being for the sake of another;
and since that [perception] cannot exist without an object, the word is here presented as the object. Therefore, [page 320]...

What [is the consequence]? From this it follows: the reason is its connection with the perception of another. This is what is meant: for that which has a perception for the sake of another, what [follows]? Its permanence. Of what, and how? We say: of everything, such as smoke and so forth. But is it not the case that the perception of smoke and so forth is also for the sake of one's own comprehension?

Let it be so; its purpose of communicating to another is also not to be rejected, because there is no contradiction, as this is present even in the case of verbal testimony (*śabda*). Furthermore, by the word "eternal" (*nitya*), what is meant is persistence over time, and not—

[The opponent states: "It is the state of being existent and having no cause. [The author replies: But surely sound is accepted as being both existent and without a cause. [The opponent says: Certainly it is so accepted;
however, that [existence] is established merely through its visibility for the sake of another. [The author asks: Why then is this distinction stated? [The opponent replies:
So that even non-eternal things like smoke might serve as an illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta). [The author asks: But surely...

Furthermore, impermanence would also follow for this [object], because it is observed to be established [as such]. For this very reason, only its persistence over a period of time is stated as the probandum (*sādhya*). And by means of that persistence over a period of time, it is established.
The non-causality of sound with respect to existence: for it was only its being seen that was suspected by others to be its cause;

and since that [seeing] serves another's purpose, it has ceased to be a cause. Therefore, it is established that sound is non-causal with respect to existence, because its causality belongs merely to its connection with the seeing that serves another's purpose. But surely—

The fact that seeing exists for the sake of another is established by relying on its non-difference from its material cause which is similar to it. True, it is established; however, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its being of such a nature. Not for anyone—

It is observed that from beginningless saṃsāra, a cognition arises in a living being such that "I am uttering [the word] similar to what was previously mentioned; this is indeed similar to that. For this very reason, they apprehend it without error. Otherwise, there would be a misconception, just as when one perceives the word *śālā* (house) instead of the word *mālā* (garland). But is it not the case that...?

Even when there is similarity, a cognitive error is observed, as in the case of the words "go" and "gāvī"; however, no such error is observed for those who grasp them as identical, nor for those who grasp their similarity. For those who know the reality, however, there is simply no arising of error at all.

What is meant by "those who know the truth" (*tattvavid*)? Those who know the truth are those who understand that *gāvī* and other such forms are corruptions (*apabhraṃśa*) of the word *go*. Regarding them, it has been stated by the commentators that the cognition of the meaning does not arise from *gāvī* and the like at all; rather, they comprehend the meaning from the word *go* alone. Nor [is this position undermined] by the beginninglessness of *saṃsāra*.
It is impossible to conceive of any "sound-ness" (śabdatā) such that linguistic convention could be established on the basis of a similar material cause.
Therefore, it is established that this linguistic convention is rooted in perception accompanied by recognition.

[Page 326] One thing has been established, while something else has been concluded: the persistence over time has been established, yet perception accompanied by recognition has been concluded; indeed, something entirely different was introduced.

And something else has also occurred; this is indeed that very same thing, for it is precisely through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that persistence over a period of time is established. And it has been stated that persistence over a period of time is cognizable by perception accompanied by recognition.
If persistence over a period of time is established by recognition alone, then why [is there mention of] the observation of another?

Was it stated that the reason is its connection with the perception of others? Precisely because the persistence over a period of time is established by recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) alone, for that very reason it was stated that the reason is its connection with the perception of others; for recognition itself [establishes] the non-different object.

It is called "perception" (darśana) and nothing else; for the nature [of perception] is established by other means of knowledge, and recognition (pratyabhijñā) is preceded by it. Furthermore, a single effort is not capable of accomplishing both its own purpose and the purpose of another.

"Because [the cognition] occurs simultaneously everywhere"—by this, he shows that the word's status as the cause for the comprehension of an object is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). What follows from this being so? [The answer is: the [cognition] occurring at another time...
Stability is established; for indeed, there can be no ascertainment of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) for that which does not persist over time.
Therefore, persistence over time is established. And this persistence over time is accompanied by recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).

It has been stated that [the word's meaning] is to be apprehended through perception. But how, then, is its status as the cause for understanding an object apprehended through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)? Because the generic form (*ākṛti*) is the word-meaning. Nor is the status of the generic form as the word-meaning apprehended through a single usage, because those [forms] which reside in substances are not perceived independently; and because there is no separate designation for those [forms] when they are not so perceived.

Because it is appropriate [to do so]. Therefore, the status of the *ākṛti* (form) as the referent of a word is to be understood solely through linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), not through direct instruction (*nirdeśa*). And since linguistic usage is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is established.

“Because of the absence of number,” this very same perception accompanied by recognition is presented once again for the purpose of demonstrating the accumulation of reasons. But what further point is established by the accumulation of reasons?

Because reasons do not depend on other reasons for the establishment of their own object? Indeed, no one does. If that is so, then the presentation of a collection [of reasons] is useless. It is not useless; for when there is a collection, firmness arises for those whose intellects require reinforcement.

And this effort is for that purpose, not for those of perfected intellect. Therefore, there is a purpose [for this treatise]. How is this suffix *kṛtvasuc* a cause for recognition? Because it is seen in the repetition of a single [action]. True, it belongs to a single [action];
however, that [repetition] belongs to the action, according to the rule "in the counting of the repetition of an action."
Because of such an injunction; for sound is not an action.
What then? It must be either a substance or a quality. This very thing, belonging to one, is being spoken of as belonging to another.
This brings to mind the maxim regarding the wealth of a maternal uncle. To this it is replied: you are ignorant of the nature of things (*vastu-svabhāva*).
For injunctions (*ādeśa*) depend upon the nature of things. And action (*kriyā*) is to be known through inference (*anumāna*). What follows from that?
It has already been stated that the essential form (*svarūpa*) of that which is to be known through inference is not perceived. Since its form is unperceived—
By what means can the non-repetition of the characteristic be understood? Is it not the case that it exists by the very same means? It exists through its effect;
therefore, let the non-repetition also arise from that. Not so; for the non-repetition [of the characteristic] can only be understood when there is a non-repetition of the effect.

Not by way of being an effect (*kārya*). For it is difficult for an effect to recur as an effect; in that case, there would simply be another effect. However, this is possible in the case of that which is made known (*jñāpya*). And it has been stated that sound is the object made known by its utterance.
Therefore, what is perceived is the repeated state of being made known of the sound, not its being produced. Hence...

Because the fruit of action is subject to destruction, it is said that there must be repetition [of practice], since the goal to be known is a single unity; this is not due to the nature of the action itself, but because of the inherent nature of the effect.
For those who have accomplished their task, there is no further performance of what has already been done. Therefore, this [repetition] pertains precisely to such a subject matter.

[The suffix] *kṛtvasuc* [is used here]. And it has been stated that the identity of the object [of action] is established through recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*). Therefore, it is logical to present the meaning of *kṛtvasuc* as the reason for its apprehension. Even though there is difference, those who are deluded by similarity [think], "That is he."
"They will say thus"—what is this that has been put forward?
This very thing has been put forward. We do not say that it was not put forward; what, then, has been refuted by this?

We do not understand what is meant by "of recognition" (*pratyabhijñāyāḥ*). This is what is being refuted here: this cognition "that [is it]" (*saḥ*) is based on the non-apprehension of difference; and the non-apprehension of difference occurs because of extreme similarity, as in the case of goats and sheep.
The difference between flames and so forth is observed; and if that difference is not apprehended, it is impossible to designate their distinctness.
And if their distinctness cannot be designated, what else remains but that "it is the very same"?
If it is argued that this is because of such designations,
[the answer is] that here it is only the failure to grasp the distinction that is at fault, as in the case of those devoid of discrimination regarding gems, pearls, and so forth; therefore,
let discrimination be resorted to in all matters, for "non-discrimination is the abode of supreme calamities."
For those who have become agitated by calamities, solitude alone is the supreme refuge; this is true as you have said.
However, in this case, there is no cause for not adopting solitude, unlike the case of flames and the like—this is [the meaning of] "because it is out of place."
This is written at length in this sūtra:
"It might be argued that since cognition and action are also recognized [through recognition], they too would consequently be eternal."
—Thus, what is this "falling of the *kūśmāṇḍas*"? Even by the subsequent [passage], the very nature of the *kūśmāṇḍas* is demonstrated: "Now, in the case of perception, they are indeed eternal."
Thus; for recognition has been stated as the reason for [an entity’s] persistence over different points of time. If that [recognition] exists even in the case of action, what is this objection?
Or if the intention is that it would result in the abandonment of one's own accepted position—that is true.

We have accepted both permanence and inferential nature [of the self]. Furthermore, recognition does not occur regarding an object that is merely inferential. Since there is no cause for the apprehension of its essential nature [in such cases], this objection is irrelevant. If you possess knowledge of our position, let it be in its entirety; why this "half-old-woman" approach? It is said in reply:
[Page 336] —If one argues that the suffix *kṛtvasuc* expresses the repetition of an action because of its having a single effect, then even the difference in causes is not established;
for the cognition of repetition does not follow from the cognition of difference. Furthermore, since their unity is being understood, there is no multiplicity even in the means of that cognition.
You yourself are indeed the object of comprehension. Thus it has been said: "For even cognition and action are recognized [as the same across time];
therefore, they too would follow as being eternal.
They might be eternal, provided they were perceptible.

For recognition does not occur with respect to an object that is not perceived. But has it not been stated that recognition is simply the non-apprehension of difference, and that this exists even in the case of cognitions and actions, since these are inferable because they are known through their effects? True.

If recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) consists in the apprehension of difference, then its grasping is [simply] recognition; for the effect produces a cognition merely to the extent that "the cause exists," but not that "it is this very same thing" or "it is something else. Recognition, however, is "this is that very same thing."
Thus it is well known in the world:
"If it is argued that the sound of today is different [from yesterday's] because of the destruction of the sound of yesterday."

What has been stated here that was not already mentioned by the author of the Bhāṣya? Indeed, it was said that when there is recognition despite non-perception, another cause must be postulated; thus, "stagnant" winds were postulated, and it was held that perception occurs upon their departure.
Conjunctions and disjunctions are the causes of disappearance; what else remains? This remains:
for that which was previously perceived, when no longer being perceived, becomes the object of the cognition "it does not exist."
For one does not leap to the apprehension that "it does not exist" regarding something that is absolutely unperceivable; even if it were perceived, [if it were not so, etc.]...

It becomes an object of cognition; thus, this very thing is accepted as being without a locus (*anāspada*). And this has been accepted [in the statement]: "The meaning of 'it does not exist' refers to that which is not in contact [with the senses].
Therefore, non-existence (*abhāva*) is either without an object or has this very [non-existent] thing as its object.
The subject must be stated. Therefore, just as in the case of flames and the like, recognition has occurred even with respect to sound.

Alas, this is a lack of discernment regarding non-apprehension; for just as non-apprehension whose object is absolutely unapprehendable is [expressed as] "it does not exist," [so too is recognition applied here].
Thus, this knowledge is not desired to arise with respect to that [object], nor likewise with respect to the object that is its referent.
Therefore, this is merely a non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) regarding the word in the interim. And so say the worldly people.

Regarding wives and other such things, people do not conclude that they "do not exist" merely on the basis of non-perception, because trust is observed when they are seen again. Therefore, this [inference] depends upon perception accompanied by recognition as its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

In that case, existence (bhāva) must be stated [as the subject]. Why? Because non-existence (abhāva) is dependent, whereas perception (pratyakṣa) is independent. This very point has been stated by the phrase "the sequence is not established. Furthermore, as for the inference here regarding all existents—
[Page 341] Regarding the statement that non-existence is understood through the absence of an object, that too is not possible here; because at the end, one observes its destruction.
[Page 342]

For this is the reason in that case: there is no destruction at the end of a sound. Therefore, this recognition is not sublated by that [argument] either; it may even sometimes cause wavering regarding jars and other such objects.
“Because of independence.
Even when recognition exists, at times— due to the non-inherent...

One might suspect impermanence on the grounds of the perception of its cause, as in the case of jars and the like; however, since that [perception of a cause] is absent here, recognition remains established, and by virtue of being the object of that recognition, the word-sound is eternal.
Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of manifestation," he dispels the suspicion that independence is unestablished.
This very suspicion is raised: "The air, having risen up, becomes sound through conjunctions and disjunctions.
And thus, the words of the Śikṣā are seen to be consistent with this: "The air attains the state of being sound."

Thus it is said. This is now refuted: if sound were composed of air, it would have to be a particular configuration of the parts of air; yet sound does not possess any such particular configurations of air-parts.

We do perceive them. But surely air is not visible to the eye. Touching is indeed a form of perception; therefore, they ought to be perceived by it; yet we do not perceive them. Therefore, recognition is uncontradicted. How then [p. 347]?
Regarding the syllables of training: because the perception of that word depends upon them, it is metaphorically designated as such.

Moreover, in this view, the syllables of the Veda are seen to be more harmonious: "By speech, which is multiform and eternal. What is the excellence here? It is the declaration of eternality by the scripture itself.
Therefore, because it is an object of the means of knowledge known as recognition, permanence is established in sound.
“Or, they would be non-expressive regarding origination, because the meaning does not have that as its cause.
“If it were innate...”
"Sound and its relationship are eternal; nevertheless, Dharma is not characterized by Vedic injunction (codanā).

What is this that has been begun? This is what has been begun: it was stated that the knowledge of the word and its meaning is innate (autpattika) based on the linguistic usage of elders (vṛddhavyavahāra). And the linguistic usage of elders consists of a sentence whose meaning is understood through other means of valid cognition (pramāṇāntara).
When someone is explaining something to another, that other person understands it;
by virtue of that understanding, even a child knows: "By this very means is that being explained."

Thus [it is said]. And comprehension (*pratipatti*) is understood through its effects, such as rejection (*hāna*) and acquisition (*upādāna*). Furthermore, rejection, acquisition, and so forth can only be understood when their objects have been cognized by another means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), not when their objects have not been so cognized. Therefore, [the object] being cognized by another means of valid knowledge—

Only in the case of the object itself can "originary nature" (autpattikatva) be understood; however, where linguistic usage is preceded by the comprehension of words, originary nature cannot be understood there. Therefore, regarding Vedic [acts] such as the Agnihotra— [p.

The inherent nature (*autpattikatva*) of words is difficult to comprehend. Therefore, the labor expended on establishing this inherent nature is useless; for those who maintain that scripture is independent, it is the inherent nature that is sought in order to establish the authority of the Veda. Furthermore, an inherent nature established through the usage of elders is not capable of being accepted as the means for understanding the meaning of the Veda.
Why is it not appropriate? For in the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*), meaning is understood from the aggregate [of words];

yet that aggregate is not employed in the Veda. Therefore, it does not function as the basis [for understanding meaning]. But surely, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is precisely from the linguistic usage of elders that the meaning of a sentence is understood as being preceded by the meanings of the individual words.

It is understood; for through the process of insertion and deletion (*āvāpoddhāra*), [the connection] is established in one instance as in: "Devadatta, bring the white cow," "Devadatta, bring the black cow," and "Viṣṇumitra, tie up the red cow."

The meaning of "white" is understood; elsewhere, the sentence-meaning is understood as that from which the meaning of "white" has been excluded and which possesses the connected meaning of "black," or as that from which the meanings of both "white" and "black" have been excluded and which possesses the connected meaning of "killing. From this, it is understood—

From words, only word-meanings are understood, not the sentence-meaning; rather, the sentence-meaning is understood through the collection of word-meanings. For otherwise, upon the removal of a single word, there would be a total lack of understanding of the entire sentence-meaning, and not merely of that specific word-meaning. Therefore, from words come word-meanings; from word-meanings [comes the sentence-meaning].

The comprehension of mutual connection [occurs as follows]: if word-meanings are understood from words, and the mutual connection [of those meanings] is understood from the word-meanings, is the sentence-meaning caused solely by the word-meanings? Yes, it is said so. Which word-meaning is the cause for which connection? [It is] every [word-meaning] for every [connection].

We reply: If that were so, then the comprehension of the meaning of every sentence would arise from every word. Alternatively, if there is a restriction, the reason must be stated: "In this manner, by such a [word], such a connection is conveyed."

Thus, we perceive no cause for this other than the usage of the elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*). Therefore, only where a word-group (*samudāya*) is employed does a word convey its own meaning; and that meaning [is conveyed] as being already connected with another word-meaning.

This conceptualization, namely "the self," is rooted in the practice and comprehension [of linguistic usage]. Therefore, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are also objects of comprehension;
for when comprehension exists, there is an understanding of insertion and deletion (*āvāpoddhāra*) in the linguistic practice of one being trained.

Furthermore, this comprehension pertains exclusively to an object already established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it is understood through the acts of avoidance and acquisition.

It has been stated that this is due to the understanding of elders. However, in cases where it is not known through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that "this word is employed in this meaning," and the meaning must be understood from usage alone, how can there be the status of being a cause (*nimittatā*)?
Is it possible to conceive of a relationship between a word and its referent based on the fact that the status of being a sign (*nimitta*) is preceded by comprehension?
For it is not the case that the comprehension of the signified (*naimittika*) arises solely from the comprehension of the sign; for when [the sign] exists...

From the perception of what comes into being, the cognition arises that "this is the cause of that," but not merely from the possibility of its existence. By whom was it stated otherwise? [It is known] precisely through the comprehension of the effect.

There is the comprehension of the cause (*nimitta*). And the meaning of the sentence—consisting of the meanings of the words—is indeed comprehended [in such injunctions] as "One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra. Therefore, in this case as well, by what means do the word and its meaning function as the cause?
Is it not excluded? But how is it understood that "the meaning of a sentence consists of the meanings of the words as related"?
Is it not from this very sentence [itself]? In that case, it has been stated that the understanding of the effect follows precisely from the understanding of the cause.

[Page 355] For in the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*), the status of being indicative (*naimittikatva*) is understood through the processes of rejection and acceptance; here, however, rejection and acceptance proceed from the word itself. Therefore, it is the opposite. But surely, even in the linguistic usage of elders—
