The practitioner understands the meaning from the sentence itself; however, a child standing nearby learns the relationship between word and meaning through the acts of rejection and acquisition. True; yet even he, after the knowledge of the relationship has arisen, understands the effect from the cause. In the case of the Veda, however, the relationship between cause and effect is not known.
Of what could the relationship be known as the state of being a cause, or of what as the state of being the effect? Or,
if an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭānumāna*) is made— that in the linguistic usage of elders there exists a causal relationship between words and word-meanings— then...

"It is observed that even in the Veda those very same word-meanings [are present]; therefore, in the Veda as well, the state of being a cause consists in being connected with their own respective meanings. If this is so, then there is no means of knowledge regarding how many [meanings] belong to which [word]. If it is argued that "as many as are perceived when a cognition occurs," then [the determination of meaning] would necessarily be preceded by cognition itself.

[The cognition] has a cause; it is not caused by the "inference from general observation" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*); nor is there a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for [the existence of] a comprehension [of such a relation], as has already been stated. Therefore, this error is based solely upon *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*. Alternatively, the comprehension of the unseen [dharma] is conventional (*sāmayikī*), preceded by the observed linguistic usage [of others]; or else, it is based on the relationship between a name and the named, which is established in the world.

[Page 357] Having done so, Vedic usage has been set in motion by some. But surely, unity of sentence (*ekavākyatva*) will be based on the unity of the task (*kārya*), and the unity of the task will result from the unity of the injunction (*niyoga*). Unity of the injunction...

And it has been stated that this is because of liberation from the [karmic] consequence. It has also been stated that the meaning of *niyoga* (the injunction) is the same in both the world and the Veda;
for by distinguishing between what is already established and what is not, [the senses of] impelling and so forth have been explained. Therefore—

Even if it were preceded by a cause (*nimitta*), there would be no fault; for inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) is established in the comprehension of a cause. This, however, is incorrect. Is the meaning of an injunction seen in the world to be a cause for the comprehension of an object because its meaning is not known through other means of knowledge? We say: "No. [For] what about that which is heard for the first time?
“Does it cause cognition?”—
this reason is not to be bypassed. If that is so, then even for the distinction of its objects, [the same applies].

Another means of valid cognition must be sought. Furthermore, in the world, it is observed that the adjuncts (anubandhas) follow the distinctions of their respective bases, but the distinction does not follow them. Therefore, mutual connection cannot be understood without first ascertaining the delimitation of usage from another source. And such a delimitation is not possible in the Veda, due to the absence of any other means of valid cognition.
[It] exists. Therefore, another philosophical system must be sought. This is not accepted by those who maintain the authority of independent scripture (*svatantrāgamavādin*).
Nor has it been stated that the comprehension of an object arises from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Consequently, [the word] is connected with the meaning of the object as it is being cognized.

The meaning of a sentence does not depend upon other means of valid cognition—this path of logic is profound. It is appropriate to deliberate: how is this to be fathomed? Therefore, those who know Brahman maintain that this single reality is understood in manifold ways through conceptual differentiation in both the world and the Veda; thus, this is indeed a phenomenal transformation (*vivarta*).

This is to be understood by those who know Brahman; that is to say, by those who know the Vedas. But how, then, is this fault not present in the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*)? For there is certainly no comprehension of oneness, given that "in the world, an object is perceived by the sense of hearing... [and so forth].

Since this has been established by the aforementioned [statement], that very point is what is called "misstated" on the grounds of contradiction with the effect (*kāryavirodha*). Does perception acquire its own nature through the effect? Let it not be perception; even inference is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

The comprehension of an object through inference is indeed logical. For you yourselves have stated that validity is everywhere inferential. How can there be oneness of an object understood through inference? Or how can there be its difference?

And without oneness, what would not be established? This [oneness] would not be established—for imagined means do not reach their goal; for if oneness were understood through scripture, the [scriptural] limitations would be merely imagined.
Nor is the understanding of oneness justified by inference—thus it has been objected. This is not a fault; for [it is established] by inference.
Having delimited the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*), one then perceives through its constituent parts a unity, as in such cases as "the cloth is white.
This very unity, which is understood from scripture, is Brahman itself when all scriptural conceptualizations have completely subsided.
"It is manifested.
As for what is said— "In common worldly usage, the term 'word' (śabda) is well-established as referring to an object perceived by the sense of hearing"—
that too contradicts the traditional scripture (*āgama*), [as in the case of the word] "cow" (*gauḥ*).
The word ‘cow’,
the object ‘cow’, and the [cognition] ‘cow’.
[Page 363] Consciousness [is one], because it is designated by a single term; for it is not possible for distinct things to be simultaneously designated by a single term.
But how is their simultaneity understood? It is through the mutual dependence of the designators, the cognitions, and the objects designated.

Because the cognition of its own nature [arises] from that, therefore, as for what was also said—that there is no cognition of a universal devoid of a reflective awareness (*avamarśa*) of its own class—that is incorrect;

for this reasoning is based on difference. Indeed, a reflective awareness occurs regarding something that exists, not regarding something imagined. And it has been stated that there is unity because of the designation by a single name.

What follows from this? This follows: it is precisely through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) that the usage of elders is said to be the cause [of linguistic convention]. And this seed of conceptual construction is stated in many ways, such as: "the first word" (*padam ādyam*).

And so forth. Therefore, the meaning is that through the cognition of the word-meanings, the refined [minds] attain non-difference. Nor does the Veda lose its authority on this account, for it has been stated that its capacity regarding the object of knowledge remains intact. Consequently, a conceptualization not based on scripture leads to transgression.

It is not Vedic [in this sense], because the Veda is intent upon the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Therefore, the innate nature (*autpattikatva*) [of the relationship between word and meaning] is established in our position.

How it is not established in the position that maintains a difference [between the word and its referent] has already been demonstrated. For this very reason, those who know the mantras describe the meanings of the mantras according to their application (*viniyoga*); for if there were a difference [between word and referent], denotation would necessarily be restricted [to the individual object].
It would follow that [the rule] "uṇādayo bahulam" and so forth would be devoid of any basis in authoritative tradition (āgama).

And this is not desired by you either. Furthermore, the instruction regarding the auxiliary sciences (*aṅgavidyā*) is purposeful; for if the distinction [between the Vedas] were established by worldly convention alone, what else would need to be taught? In our view, however, the distinction follows from scripture (*āgama*); and because scripture is infinite, the instruction is meaningful. Therefore, this designation of distinctions [is justified].

There are distinctions among the worldly, the Vedic, the archaic meter (chandas), and the common language (bhāṣā), as well as various traditions (āgama). By someone, in a certain context, that very same [action] is presented as being delimited;
for this very reason, the offering on eleven or twelve potsherds (*kapāla*) constitutes a single ritual act. Otherwise, if a distinction were perceived, [the acts would be separate].

To speak of them as one is mere idle chatter; this applies not only here, but also to the entire composition of the discourse. Furthermore, since the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*) is understood through its effect (*kārya*), and since that effect is one, there is no multiplicity of designations.

It is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, although there is a difference in the comprehension of sentences and compounds, the mention of the word *vā* (or) serves to prevent an equal conceptualization [of them as identical], and it is appropriate for the purpose of making known the alternative possibilities (*vikalpa*) regarding the traditional teachings (*āgama*). Otherwise, the entity itself would be the cause of cessation. For this very reason, the determination of the power that functions under the influence of the denotable object (*abhidheya*) belongs to nouns and verbs.

Regarding the suffixes *sarga* and *nipāta*: for if there were a difference [between them], the difference in their essential nature (*svarūpa*) would be ultimate (*pāramārthika*). In that case, when there is recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), [the forms] "vilambate" and "pralambate" [would not be identical].
The term ‘vipra’ would not signify difference; likewise in the case of [the suffixes] *bhavat* and so forth.

For those who maintain that [the meaning of a compound] consists merely of its constituent phonemes (*varṇamātravādin*), there occurs a connection between two words—as in "the king’s man’s elephant"—but not as in "the elephant of the king’s man. Likewise, there is "this belongs to Upagu" or "this belongs to the offspring," but not "this belongs to the descendant of Upagu" (*aupagava*). And so it is with the instrument (*karaṇa*) and by means of the instrument.

Thus, there is both the production and non-production of case-endings (*vibhakti*). Likewise, *sub*-derived verbal roots (such as *aśva* and *gardabha*) function as both nouns and verbs—as in *aśvaḥ*, *gardabhaḥ*, *aśvati*, and *gardabhati*. Furthermore, the family of the letter *a* (*avarṇakula*), which has eighteen varieties, serves for the comprehension of meaning. Otherwise, because the entity would be a single unity, there would be either comprehension of all meanings or no comprehension at all.

The systematic establishment [of objects] is not tenable. When an object is already cognized through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), a further apprehension of it is false—as in the cases "the sandalwood is fragrant" and "the breeze is cool. [In these cases,] fragrance belongs to the sandalwood and coolness to the breeze.

This must indeed be so. For prepositions and particles sometimes serve as qualifiers, sometimes are meaningless, and sometimes have contrary meanings; this would not be possible if they were non-existent. Furthermore, since the meaning of a sentence is preceded by the meaning of its constituent words, a determination [of the sentence-meaning] based on them would be impossible to state. Moreover, if there were a difference in the words, the meaning of the words would be destroyed.

And if there were meaninglessness, how could there be syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*)? And how could there be knowledge of the division [of words]? There would be only the addition of phonemes (*varṇopajana*).

However, under the view that it is a conceptualization based on tradition (*āgamavikalpa*), everything is coherent. But from what does the comprehension of this conceptualization based on tradition arise?
If [it is argued that this is so], then it is from another scripture itself. As it has been said: "Even the knowledge of the sages is preceded by scripture.
And its lack of a first beginning can be established because the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) is beginningless.
To proceed: this independence (*anapekṣatā*) is the cause of validity. On the view that [the Veda] is distinct [from human cognition], all of this is inconsistent.
Furthermore, the Veda, which functions primarily as knowledge, demonstrates the Veda’s quality of imparting unimpeded comprehension.
How so? [The Upanishads state: "Now, that which is small is mortal."
"Then that which is the earth is immortal"—what is that "small" (alpa)? It is limitation (avaccheda); it is the limitation of that which is to be conceptualized.
It is seen, but not so the reality (*tattva*). Everything beginning with "as far as the reach of speech" is logically consistent.
It is so; otherwise, there would be contradiction. And where there is contradiction, there is a lack of authority.

Therefore, those who know the scripture explain this as being consistent with the one [Brahman], which is the mass of Brahman (*brahmarāśi*). This is the scripture; this is that reality (*tattva*); these are the knowers of Brahman who understand it thus. Therefore, turn away—

[Objection: From this very grasping of difference, which follows along with cyclic existence, it may be argued that even here, the mastery of usage through the elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*) is of no help at all. If conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) proceed from scripture (*āgama*), what is the use of the usage of elders?
Or, if by means of mastery of the usage of elders they do not engage in conceptual constructions, but rather understand the conceptual constructions of scripture as being non-conceptual; [then...]

This is equally true even regarding the conventional usage of distinctions. If conceptual constructions are understood solely through scripture, then what is the use of comprehending the causal signs (nimitta) for those who have already mastered the linguistic conventions of elders? Therefore, this [point] also [applies].
The position [you propose] ultimately results in the very same view as the theory of difference (*bheda*). Now, there is this other alternative:

just as genus (*jāti*) and quality (*guṇa*) are perceived to have a relation to a single substance because they both reside in one and the same substance, so too, when a word for a genus and a word for a quality are uttered in proximity, it is understood that they have a single referent by means of that [single substance]. If this is argued, it is not so; for in the case of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*),...

If it is argued that because understanding occurs as a mere sign (*nimitta*), the understanding must likewise be a mere sign, and thus there is meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*); we reply that meaninglessness is not a reason for the understanding of another object. Therefore, this [objection] is indeed meaningless.
The laborious assertion of an innate relationship between word and meaning based on the usage of elders is therefore unnecessary.

Consequently, it remains established that the aforementioned nature of the relationship—whether it be artificial or conventional—is the case. [Objection: "Even if the word and the relationship are innate and eternal, nevertheless, dharma is not characterized by Vedic injunction (codanā)."
—Thus, it is to be asserted that the linguistic usage of the elders lacks a [valid] basis in the case of Vedic usage; as it has been said:
“For the injunction is a sentence. Indeed, it is not understood from the words ‘from the Agnihotra, heaven arises.’”
The understanding that is said to arise from this statement is merely a subordinate element for the expression of the reason; nor is this a collective whole.

It is established through the usage of the elders, which is employed in the Śruti. Therefore, the previously mentioned lack of a [new] cause has been described as the meaning of this Bhāṣya: "For these words are employed, and their meaning is eternal."
For thus, in the linguistic usage of the elders, the innate nature of words is established as the cause with respect to that very effect; here,
however,
it is not established at all with respect to the comprehension of another effect.

The state of being a mere sign (nimittabhāva). Why? Because the aggregate is not employed [independently]. This being so, artificiality (kṛtrimatva) has been described. And since "the meaning of the sentence is not merely the word-meanings," there is a mutual lack of syntactic connection (parasparānanvayitā).

He demonstrates this: for it is the state of mutual connection that is called a "particular" (*viśeṣa*). By the statement, "A word functions with respect to a universal (*sāmānya*), whereas a sentence [functions] with respect to a particular," the conventional derivation of the term *pada* (word) is rendered purposeless.

Thus it has been stated; and the detailed explanation regarding this has already been given previously: "Nor is there comprehension of the meaning of a sentence from the meaning of individual words, because there is no connection [between them]."

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might object: there certainly is a relationship between the word-meanings and the sentence-meaning, because it is precisely their mutual connection that constitutes the sentence-meaning. Indeed, a mutual connection devoid of actual usage cannot be apprehended; thus, the aforementioned lack of comprehension is based on this very commentary: "In its absence..."
"If, when some related meaning has been understood, another meaning were to be understood [thereby], then everything would be understood once one thing is understood"—
this is the reason for the sentence-meaning not having the word-meanings as its cause.
And this has been described: "Even from a sentence that is not [intentionally] employed, when there is no [intended] connection, the comprehension of meaning occurs through its own inherent nature."
By this [statement], it has been described that the Veda demonstrates a unity of injunction (niyoga) free from secondary adjuncts (anubandha):
"The word would overstep its own nature as a dharma; nor is it a property of words that meaning is understood from a word that is not employed."
Thus, he demonstrates that the subordinate elements (anubandhas) follow the purpose (kārya), as has been stated: "Indeed, no one understands any meaning from a word heard for the first time."
—Thus, the contradiction with the *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* [inference] previously mentioned has been stated. To this it is replied: This is a property of the word (*pada*), not [of the object].
[Page 377]

"It is a property of the sentence; for people are seen to comprehend [the meaning] even from a sentence heard for the first time."—[If this is so,] how then is there a lack of comprehension of the meaning? We know that comprehension arises precisely from the mastery of the meanings of individual words alone.
The point that "the usage of elders is the cause for understanding the meaning of the Veda"—this which was previously stated has been introduced by this commentary [as follows]:

"This is not so; if they were to understand from hearing it for the first time, then everyone would understand—both those who know the meanings of words and others; however, those who do not know the meanings of words do not understand."

Thus it is said. For indeed, when words are not employed in common worldly usage, the meaning cannot be understood from the aggregate [of sounds]. As for the claim that those who know the meanings of word-components do understand it—

This should be understood as being due to the aforementioned error of *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* (inference based on general observation). [Objection: "But surely, even those who know word-meanings perceive the relation of sentence-meaning as being indeed uncreated (*akṛtaka*); for those refined by the knowledge of word-meanings will perceive it, just as they perceive that very same meaning a second time and so forth."

"By hearing"—what confusion is there here? Rather than [assuming] a conceptual construction based on scripture, it is better that it be simply a cause (*nimitta*), just as in common usage the hearing of a second or subsequent [word] is a cause. This is the meaning previously described.
“We say no; for if the final phoneme of a sentence, accompanied by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the preceding phonemes,
conveys a meaning distinct from the word-meanings, then what benefit could possibly be derived at that time from the knowledge of those word-meanings?”

—Thus, the meaning is that the aforementioned lack of a [specific] cause (*animittatva*) regarding the Veda is the same even in the case of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). [Objection: "But in this way, it will be possible:
for a word denoting a universal, such as ‘cow’..."
Whether it be "horse" or "white," the former is the general term and the latter is the qualifier.
When a word such as "black" or "white" falls near [the other words],
then the meaning of the sentence is understood.

Thus, that which was stated—namely, that the cause for the arising of a single cognition with respect to two objects is based on the unity of their effect—that has been presented. [The opponent replies: "No; for how could it be [the case] that 'cow'..."
Thus, from a word expressing a universal, such as "cow" or "horse," [cognition arises] with respect to all cows or all horses.

"And would the cognition arising from hearing, as it approaches [the meaning] in accordance with the sentence, ever deviate from some specific [particularity]? By this, he has restated what was previously mentioned: that because linguistic usage is learned only through the causes [of meaning], there would result only an understanding of isolated word-meanings during the learning of usage, and not their mutual syntactic connection. However, the "objective cause" (arthanimitta) is that which pertains to the object itself.

It is not verbal; rather, this is being investigated as a verbal matter. And in that regard, it has been stated that the status of being a cause belongs only to that which is actually employed in usage. Furthermore, in the acquisition of the meaning of usage, there is no [functioning] of the word through the exclusion of other word-meanings.

The fact that [the word] has its own meaning as its cause is observed, by which it can be said that the cognition regarding all female cows (*gavī*) is excluded from the word through the employment of another term. But if this is so, will there not be pointlessness (*ānarthakya*)?
Let it be so; for this pointlessness cannot be construed as being directed toward another meaning—it is indeed pointlessness itself.

For otherwise that would not be the case; therefore, the relationship [between word and meaning] is artificial. Its independence has been set aside. And this reason has been established: the Veda is a product because it consists of sentences.
[Page 382] “The recitation of those [words] that denote substances is for the sake of action, because the purpose [of the Veda] has that as its cause.
To this, it is replied:

The usage of elders would lack efficacy as a means [of knowledge] if there were a difference in the word-meanings themselves; it is merely the process of insertion and deletion (*āvāpoddhāra*) that is different. Why? Because no difference is perceived between the word-meanings of Vedic and worldly contexts. Why is this, which has already been answered, stated again? For the mutual connection of word-meanings [is what constitutes a sentence].
It has been stated that this is the meaning of the sentence, not the meanings of the individual words; therefore, the recognition of word-meanings is not the cause of syntactic connection (*anvaya*).
Furthermore, it has been stated that no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is employed in this regard. Consequently, the syntactic connection is devoid of actual application.
[Objection: It is seedless. You are ignorant of words and their meanings, yet you are fond of your mother. How so?

Because word-meanings are never perceived anywhere without being mutually connected, at least with the sense of existence (*asti*). [Reply: What of it? This follows from that. For the linguistic usage of words and meanings exists precisely for the sake of comprehending those [connections].
And in common usage, insertion and extraction occur precisely according to the interconnection [of words]. Therefore, there is the expression of an interconnected meaning.

Because the understanding arises from the mutual connection, there is a connection [between the word and its meaning]. What will result from this? It will be that the word is not said to be one that expresses unrelated things; and consequently, it will be understood in common worldly usage that the word denotes an action (*kārya*), namely, an injunction (*niyoga*).

“For I act when impelled by the teacher”—thus it has been shown. But surely, in common worldly usage, commands and the like are also understood. These, however, are merely limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), not the primary meanings of the words. By what, then, are these [commands] considered limiting adjuncts?

What is its name? For adventitious attributes (*upādhi*), being merely peripheral, establish the specific referent of a word through the observation of usage alone, just as the state of being an animal is established for that which is denoted by the term *dṛtihari*. In this same way, this injunction (*niyoga*)—whether equal, inferior, or superior—...

When [an action] is employed with these [words], it receives designations such as "command" (*preṣaṇa*) and so forth. However, the meaning of the word is its capacity to instigate (*pravartakatva*), because this is never abandoned in any case. Therefore, this is a designation of *niyoga* (the mandate). And when there is a designation of *niyoga*, its connection with the means (*sādhana*) is understood; and when there is a designation of the means, its connection with the end to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is understood. Therefore...

This has been stated: it is logical that those [words] which have become established in their own respective meanings serve as the cause for the comprehension of their mutual connection. But surely, this is only appropriate to say when there is actual usage (*prayoga*). By whom was it said that it applies when there is no usage?
For worldly usage is indeed observed in such cases, and the Vedic usages are likewise the same.

Therefore, this application [of the reason] is directed toward those very things that have become such [i.e., possessing the property to be proven]. If that is so, then the cognition of the effect arises from the cause.
